This is further supported by the results of the AR1ZE study that used the US Flatiron Health database to evaluate survival outcomes in patients with stage III NVRD disease after PDS versus a PRIMA-like cohort.[93] The observed real-world median TTNT was doubled for the stage III NVRD cohort compared to the PRIMA-like cohort (22.5 months vs 11.7 months). Similarly, the real-world median PFS was also 2.5 times longer for the stage III NVRD compared to the PRIMA-like cohort (25.2 months vs 10.1 months )[93] Since patients with good prognosis and the potential for complete cytoreduction are more likely to receive PDS (Section 1.4.2.2), the AR1ZE findings demonstrate that patients with stage III NVRD after PDS, who were excluded from the PRIMA trial, have a significantly better prognosis and extended survival when treated with niraparib.[93] These results reinforce that the outcomes from PRIMA could have been consistent with those of other PARPi monotherapies (olaparib, rucaparib) if it had included both high- and low-risk patients. 

## **External validation of PRIME representativeness for low-risk and high-risk patients** . 

As the PRIME study accounted for both patient groups, it resulted in a notably longer Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 109 -->

median PFS in patients treated with niraparib compared to those in PRIMA, which only included high-risk patients. Among the RWE studies identified in SLR, two studies (RENI1,[94] Chen 2024[95] ) suggest that PRIME is a reasonable representation of what PRIMA outcomes would look like if all patients, both high-risk and low-risk, were included. Both studies demonstrated PFS results closer to those of PRIME and notably higher than those of PRIMA, providing further external validation for PRIME in the real world. 

The RENI-1 study prospectively enrolled 227 patients with newly diagnosed OC who received niraparib as a 1L maintenance therapy in China.[94] With the median follow-up of 23.9 months, the median PFS was not reached any patient group (overall, BRCA and HRd), while the 12-month PFS rates were 69.1%, 87.2% and 76.2%, respectively.[94] Chen 2024 was a retrospective study based in China that evaluated the efficacy and safety of niraparib (n=60) or olaparib (n=104) as a 1L maintenance therapy for the treatment of newly diagnosed eOC[95] Niraparib was primarily administered to patients with BRCAwt (86.7%), while olaparib was predominantly given to patients with BRCAm (88.5%). The median PFS for patients treated with niraparib was 22.1 months (95% CI not evaluable), which was longer than in the PRIMA study and comparable to PRIME (Sections 2.4.2.1 and 2.5.2.1).[95] Based on Chen 2024, making a direct comparison between olaparib and niraparib was not feasible due to differences in baseline characteristics.[95] 

## **Evidence further supporting the comparability of PARPis and the class effect** 

One study comparing niraparib and olaparib was identified in the SLR (Kim 2024[96] ), which further supported the comparability of niraparib with other PARPi monotherapies and suggests a class effect for PARPi in comparable populations (i.e., including both low-risk and high-risk patients). 

Kim 2024 was a retrospective, multicentre cohort study that included data from three Korean institutions to compare PFS in 161 patients with stage III/IV OC with BRCA1/2 mutations who received cytoreductive surgery followed by 1L PBC. The study employed a 3:1 propensity score matching approach to ensure comparable populations for niraparib and olaparib.[96] After matching, no significant difference was observed between the Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 110 -->

olaparib and niraparib groups for median PFS (log-rank test p=0.855; HR: 1.08; 95% CI: 0.47, 2.52; p=0.854), time to subsequent therapy (HR: 1.20; 95% CI: 0.51, 2.81; p=0.682) and OS (HR: 0.42; 95% CI: 0.01, 17.61; p=0.649), reinforcing the comparability of niraparib with olaparib and indicating that niraparib offers similar efficacy to PARPi monotherapies when used in comparable populations.[96] 

## _**2.8.1.2 Key highlights of niraparib’s safety**_ 

## **Dose individualisation and real-world safety outcomes** 

The protocol amendment in PRIMA, which introduced ISD, was associated with reduced AEs (Section 2.4.7.4). This finding is further supported by UK-specific RWE from MONITOR, which confirms that ISD is widely adopted in clinical practice, with the majority of patients initiating niraparib treatment at 200 mg.[25] 

MONITOR-UK is a UK-based observational study that included patients with newly diagnosed or recurrent OC who received niraparib as a maintenance treatment.[25] Of the 319 patients enrolled, 165 (52%) were 1L, with 16% receiving an initial dose of 300 mg niraparib and 79% receiving 200 mg.[25] Grade ≥3 TEAEs were reported in 33% (n=103) of all patients (1L and recurrent),[25] which is lower than that observed in PRIMA (Section 2.4.7.4). The most common Grade ≥3 TEAEs were hypertension, anaemia, low neutrophil count, and low platelet count, occurring in 14%, 8%, 7% and 7% of all patients, respectively.[25] Adverse events of special interest were rare and included secondary cancer diagnosis (n=4), pneumonitis (n=2), AML (n=1), and MDS (n=1). Despite the predominance of 200 mg dosing, dose reductions occurred in nearly 50% of patients, with few discontinuations reported (5%).[25] 

Thus the MONITOR study demonstrates that niraparib can be considered a manageable and tolerable option for maintenance treatment in OC and supports the use of ISD in clinical practice, emphasising the importance of personalised dosing to optimise patient outcomes and limit risk of AEs. 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 111 -->

Furthermore, subgroup results in PRIMA (Section C.1.4.1)[74] and the NOVA study[80] for recurrent OC indicated similar efficacy for individualised and fixed dosing. RWE data also support that niraparib's effectiveness is independent of dose.[97,98] Therefore, ISD helps reduce AEs without compromising efficacy. 

## **2.8.2 SACT dataset** 

The previous NICE appraisal recommended the commissioning of niraparib through the Cancer Drugs Fund (CDF) to allow managed access and support additional data collection to address clinical uncertainty.[26] Patients with advanced OC under the CDF were identified through the NHS England Blueteq[®] system, and real-world data were collected via the SACT database.[19] 

Between 15 January 2021 and 31 August 2024, 3,100 CDF applications for niraparib were identified in the Blueteq[®] system, with 2,785 unique patients included in the SACT analysis. Data for patients who had a deleterious or suspected deleterious BRCA germline and/or somatic BRCA mutation (N=90) and those who didn’t (N=2,695) were analysed separately.[19] Notably, test results for HRD status were unavailable for the majority of patients (83% to 87%). Most patients in both groups initiated niraparib treatment on 200 mg daily (87% and 83% in BRCAm and BRCAwt, respectively), and more than half of patients (BRCAm: 62%, BRCAwt: 54%) had a complete response to PBC.[19] Additionally, the majority of patients had never been exposed to bevacizumab as part of induction therapy (87% in BRCAm and 91% in BRCAwt).[19] Detailed patient characteristics are shown in Table 30.[19]

## **2.10 Strengths of the clinical evidence** 

Niraparib is the only PARPi among those approved for maintenance treatment after 1L PBC in advanced OC with efficacy and safety confirmed in two high-quality phase III RCTs – PRIMA and PRIME.[12,13] 

PRIMA was designed as an all-comer trial, enrolling patients regardless of their BRCA or HRD status.[12] This inclusive approach allows for a broader understanding of niraparib’s efficacy across various biomarker subgroups, thereby making the findings more applicable to a broader patient population.[26] 

PRIMA also stands out among PARPi trials for disproportionately enrolling those with the highest risk of progression and the greatest unmet need.[12] In contrast to SOLO-1[17] and ATHENA-MONO[18] , PRIMA specifically excluded patients with the lowest risk of relapse (i.e., stage III patients with NVRD after PDS) who are known to have a more favourable prognosis and were well represented in the previous PARPi trials (Section 1.4.2.2).[12] Therefore, the PRIMA trial aimed to investigate the utility of PARPi therapy in a population with the highest risk of progression and greatest unmet need. 

The PRIME[13] study complements findings from the PRIMA trial by providing information on niraparib's efficacy regardless of risk of relapse. Notably, PRIME included patients who were not assessed in the PRIMA study (stage III with no residual disease after PDS) and used individualised starting doses, in accordance with the dosing label, from the beginning of the trial, consistent with UK clinical practice. The outcomes across PRIMA and PRIME were similar, demonstrating consistent results between these two pivotal trials and highlighting the efficacy and safety of niraparib in different patient populations and study designs. Notably, PRIME reported numerically longer medians compared to PRIMA, likely reflecting the mix of high- and low-risk patients enrolled in the study. 

In summary, the clinical evidence for niraparib is robust, demonstrating its efficacy in a broad range of patients with advanced OC, including those in the high-risk group, and underscoring its potential as a valuable PARPi therapy.

## **2.11 Interpretation of clinical effectiveness and safety evidence** 

**Impact of niraparib on PFS:** Across both the PRIMA[12,16] and PRIME[13] pivotal trials, the efficacy of niraparib was demonstrated in prolonging the PFS in the 1L maintenance setting regardless of biomarker status. Each of the trials met their primary endpoints, with the more mature PRIMA[12,16] trial showing a sustained and consistent PFS benefit across the primary, interim and final analysis data cuts.[12-14] The magnitude of benefit was greatest in the BRCAm and HRd populations; however, niraparib also demonstrated benefit in BRCAwt and HRp patients, who represent those with the highest unmet needs and poorest prognosis.[12,16,46,49] The improvement in PFS in the PRIMA trial was robust across various prognostic factors, including stage and surgical outcome.[12,16] 

Although PRIMA focused on a higher-risk population, evidence from PRIME[13] and RWE[82 ] demonstrated clinically meaningful benefits for niraparib in a broader population that also included low-risk patients, thus supporting niraparib’s use in the relevant population for this appraisal (in line with its marketing authorisation). In PRIME,[13] the inclusion of lowerrisk patients resulted in a median PFS for niraparib that was nearly twice as long as in PRIMA[12,16] (24.8 months for niraparib in PRIME compared to 13.8 months for niraparib in PRIMA), despite a similar median PFS for placebo in both studies (8.3 months in PRIME and 8.2 months in PRIMA), which demonstrates that niraparib is effective across a broader range of patient risk profiles. Similar results were obtained in the US-based AR1ZE[82 ] study, which showed that median real-world PFS in the stage III with no residual disease after PDS cohort was significantly longer (25.2 months) than the PRIMA-like cohort (10.1 months; p<0.001). 

**Impact of niraparib on OS and other secondary outcomes:** PRIMA was a positive trial that successfully met its primary endpoint of PFS.[12,16] However, it did not achieve the secondary endpoint of OS, with no differences observed in OS between niraparib and placebo in the ITT population or the subgroups analysed.[12,16] This lack of OS benefit has also been observed in other trials in aOC,[14,17,64] where extended post-progression 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 120 -->

survival can obscure treatment effects and make it more challenging to demonstrate statistically significant differences between arms. 

As PRIMA was designed with PFS as the primary endpoint, differences in postprogression treatments between treatment arms and patient management may have impacted OS outcomes. Additionally, potential unblinding after progression to help inform treatment decisions post-progression could introduce performance bias in the assessment of post-progression outcomes such as OS. 

Despite not achieving statistical significance for OS, the median OS observed in PRIMA was numerically high; this is particularly noteworthy given the high-risk patient population. Furthermore, the survival outcomes were consistent with the results reported for a similarly high-risk subgroup in the PAOLA-1 trial investigating olaparib as an add-on to bevacizumab in the 1L setting; in the intent-to-treat (ITT) population, PRIMA reported a median OS of 46.6 months with niraparib, compared to 42.2 months for olaparib plus bevacizumab in PAOLA-1, and in the homologous recombination deficient (HRd) population, PRIMA reported a median OS of 71.9 months with niraparib, compared to 67 months for olaparib plus bevacizumab in PAOLA-1. It must be noted that given the differences in trial designs, patient populations, and baseline characteristics these results should be interpreted with caution.[16] 

**Comparison with other PARPis:** There are no direct comparisons between niraparib and the relevant comparators (olaparib and rucaparib) in a clinical trial setting in 1L aOC maintenance. Therefore, several exploratory ITCs were conducted despite the ITC feasibility assessment deeming these comparisons inappropriate and fundamentally flawed, in order to aid decision making (Section 2.7.4). 

The exploratory ITCs showed no statistically significant differences in PFS outcomes when comparing niraparib (PRIMA) to olaparib (SOLO-1). While the HR point estimate nominally favoured olaparib, likely influenced by unadjusted imbalances in prognostic factors between trial populations, the wide confidence interval supports equivalence 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 121 -->

between the treatments. Real-world evidence further supports comparable outcomes between olaparib and niraparib in BRCAm patients receiving maintenance therapy, showing no statistically significant differences in PFS, OS, or TFST.[96] Additionally, English SACT data[19] revealed that OS Kaplan-Meier curves for niraparib and olaparib overlap during the first 27 months, with nearly identical proportions of patients alive at key milestones (6–24 months), further indicating equivalence between the two treatments and reinforcing the potential PARPi class effect (Section B.3.2.6). 

Similarly, exploratory ITCs comparing niraparib (PRIME) to rucaparib (ATHENA-MONO) showed no statistically significant differences in PFS or OS outcomes. While the HR point estimate nominally favoured niraparib for the ITT population, the difference was neither clinically nor statistically significant (Section 2.7). 

**Safety of niraparib** : Niraparib was generally well tolerated in both PRIMA and PRIME, demonstrating an acceptable and predictable safety profile, with no new safety signals identified.[13] 

It is noteworthy to mention that the frequency of AEs observed in PRIMA was significantly higher compared to PRIME (Section 2.4.7.4 and Section 2.5.7.4) and the more recent UK-specific real-world data (Section 2.8.1.2), likely reflecting the impact of individualised dosing regimens implemented after the PRIMA protocol amendment (Section 2.4.1). In the MONITOR-UK study, where patients started on individualised dosing, Grade ≥3 TEAEs were reported in fewer patients than in the PRIMA trial, with the most common being hypertension (14%), anaemia (8%), low neutrophil count (6%), and low platelet count (6%).[25] 

A post-hoc analysis of PRIMA data investigated the efficacy and safety of the individualised starting dose versus the fixed starting dose. No significant differences in efficacy were observed between the two dosing strategies, both in the overall population and the HRd/HRp populations. Furthermore, ISD was associated with a lower incidence of AEs, highlighting improved tolerability without compromising efficacy (xxxxxx 45,

Appendix C.1.4.1).[74] Similar conclusions were reported by a real-world evidence study, which found no differences in efficacy between ISD and FSD.[97] 

In summary, the PRIMA and PRIME trials, along with real-world evidence studies, demonstrate that individualised dosing of niraparib improves safety versus fixed dosing, while maintaining efficacy.

## **3 Cost-effectiveness** 

## **3.1 Cost-effectiveness summary** 

- For the purpose of this submission, a de novo model uses a 3-health state partitioned survival structure, as a 4-state model is considered less relevant given that postprogression pathways are similar across first-line PARPi monotherapies 

   - Furthermore, a 4-state model results in additional complexity as well as further data requirements which would not have been feasible given the absence of suitable PFS2 data for the relevant comparators 

- In addition to standard parametric models, flexible spline models were explored for PFS and OS extrapolations. The most appropriate curves were selected based on clinical feedback and the NICE DSU methods guide[99,100] 

- In line with previous PARPi NICE appraisals,[27,28,70] patients alive and progression-free after 10 years were considered to be in long-term remission (“cured”) and were assumed to follow general population mortality thereafter. No adjustments were made to the OS extrapolations, which continued until the OS curve intersected with the PFS curve 

- ITCs and RWE from SACT[19] data suggest no clinically meaningful differences in efficacy outcomes between niraparib and the relevant comparators, highlighting the potential for a ‘class effect’ among these treatments; this class effect is more established in the second line setting for aOC where trials are more comparable. Therefore, PARPi equivalence was considered in the base case 

- Relative dose intensity was accounted for to reflect dose reductions 

   - It is important to note that cost savings are realised only with niraparib, as it is formulated exclusively as 100 mg tablets; therefore, monthly costs depend on the average dose received 

   - In contrast, rucaparib and olaparib are available in different strength formulations which are priced identically, meaning dose reductions do not result in corresponding cost savings 

   - Therefore, dose reductions were only considered for niraparib in the base case, with the impact of considering RDI for comparators explored in scenario analyses 

- Economic analyses demonstrate that niraparib is a cost-effective treatment option in the first-line maintenance setting, regardless of a patient’s BRCA status 

- Its availability in routine commissioning will ensure physicians and patients continue to have the choice to select the most appropriate PARPi treatment based on the individual patient characteristics and PARPi safety profile

## **3.2 Published cost effectiveness studies** 

A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted to identify published 1L maintenance aOC economic models. The SLR was conducted[101] according to the reporting standards of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA),[102] general methodological requirements outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions[103] , and key health technology assessment (HTA) bodies, such as NICE[104] and Canada’s Drug Agency (CDA)[105] By following the methodologies of these HTA bodies, the SLR complied with the general SLR requirements of most other HTA bodies. Details on the search strategy and inclusion criteria are presented in Appendix E:. The focus of this section is on the UK-related SLR findings, as it is thought these are the most relevant to inform the current appraisal. 

Forty-nine cost-effectiveness studies were identified in the SLR for patients with stage III and IV OC treated in the 1L maintenance setting with PR or CR prior to 1L treatment. Of the included studies, 21 were technology appraisals of which 6 were NICE technology appraisal submissions (niraparib, NICE TA673[26] 2019; olaparib versus RS, NICE TA598[106] 2019 and NICE TA962[70] 2024; olaparib + bevacizumab versus bevacizumab, NICE TA693[107] 2021 and NICE TA946[70] 2024; rucaparib versus placebo, NICE TA1055[28] , 2024). 

Across the 49 studies, cost-effectiveness was primarily analysed using a Markov (n=11), semi-Markov model structure (n=6), or a partitioned survival analysis with a minimum of three health states (n=30), with the remaining two studies appearing to conduct trialbased cost-effectiveness analyses. Most frequently, the health states assessed were progression-free, progressive disease, and death. However, some studies incorporated additional health states to account for multiple disease progressions[108-114] as well as one study that utilised disease-specific health states such as haematological complications.[115] 

Among the previous NICE technology appraisal submissions, (TA673[26] , TA598[106] , TA962[27,70] , TA693[107] , TA946[70] and TA1055[28] ) all utilised a partitioned survival models with either three or four health states (i.e., differentiated according to inclusion of PFS2). Table 34 summarises the key modelling considerations for the relevant NICE submissions identified. The approach to model efficacy varied across the three reviewed NICE TAs. For PFS, TA946[70] (olaparib + bevacizumab) and TA962[27,70] (olaparib) used mixture cure models (MCMs) for PFS to capture long-term responders/survivors. Splines were also included in the exploratory analysis in TA946[70] (olaparib + bevacizumab). TA1055[28] used the PFS K-M curve followed by standard parametric extrapolation, with flexible parametric spline models also being explored for PFS in the bevacizumab-ineligible population. Both TA946[27] (olaparib + bevacizumab) and TA962[27] (olaparib) considered a landmark cure point at 5 years to justify MCM. PFS2 was modelled using standard parametric fits across all TAs, with the Evidence Assessment Group (EAG) requesting MCMs for PFS2 in 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 126 -->

TA962[27] (olaparib) to be consistent with the PFS modelling approach. OS was frequently modelled using standard parametric extrapolation (TA946[70] , TA962[27] , and TA1055[28] ), with the EAG requesting MCMs (TA962[27] ) or splines (TA946[70] ) to align with the PFS extrapolation approach. All reviewed TAs adopted a lifetime horizon (40-47 years) and monthly cycles. 

A comparable OS between the active arm and the comparator arm was observed in TA1055[28] for rucaparib. In TA962[70] (olaparib), the EAG was concerned that OS was similar between olaparib and RS until ~42 months, after which OS separation was observed. A robust clinical rationale could not be provided by the company to explain it, but the overall OS HR (0.55 [0.40 – 0.76]) indicated a survival benefit associated with olaparib use. In TA946[70] (olaparib + bevacizumab), PAOLA-1 long-term data supported olaparib + bevacizumab OS benefit vs. bevacizumab (HR OS=0.62 [0.45-0.85]) and was thus reflected in the economic model, with EAG-company discussion more focused on which cure fraction/long-term survival extrapolation was more appropriate rather than whether olaparib + bevacizumab results in a survival benefit. In the rucaparib appraisal, OS was still immature, with no KM curves separation observed in the March 2022 data cut (OS HR = 0.96 [0.63-1.47]) and a not statistically significant difference in OS observed in the 2023 data-cut (HR OS = 0.83 [0.58=1.17]). The committee concluded that, despite ATHENA-MONO not showing yet a slowing of PFS hazards to support long-term survivorship, it is likely that some people having rucaparib would experience long-term remission in line with other PARP inhibitors (based on clinical expert opinion). This was reflected in the choice of PFS extrapolations (i.e. log-logistic/log-normal distributions) and OS distributions (log-normal distribution), with the committee (based on clinical expert opinion) assuming the same hazard of death for rucaparib and olaparib + bevacizumab long-term.

## **3.3 Economic analysis** 

A _de novo_ model was developed to assess the cost-effectiveness, using an NHS and PSS perspective, of niraparib against approved treatments in the 1L maintenance setting for patients who have responded to PBC. 

The key features of the de novo model are described in the sub-sections that follow. 

## **3.3.1 Patient population** 

The patient population of the cost-effectiveness model (CEM) is aligned with the NICE scope for this appraisal and the marketing authorisation for niraparib (Section 1.1). The PRIMA trial population forms the basis of the clinical evidence for this evaluation, which considered: adult females (≥18 years of age) who are newly diagnosed with stage III or IV high-grade serous or endometrioid ovarian, primary peritoneal, or fallopian tube cancer (collectively referred to as OC) who responded to 1L PBC. 

The two populations of interest identified for the submission are: 

- **BRCAm** : patients with a BRCA mutation, as defined in the PRIMA trial[16,82] 

- **BRCA wild-type (BRCAwt)** : patients without a BRCA mutation, as defined in the PRIMA trial[16,82] 

As described in Sections 1.4.3.1 to 1.4.3.3, the standard of care therapy, and therefore relevant comparator, differs based on BRCA status, with olaparib currently recommended by NICE for BRCAm patients and rucaparib for BRCAwt patients. Therefore, the CEM included separate analyses for the BRCAm and BRCAwt populations to enable comparison of niraparib vs. each of the available PARPi monotherapies, according to BRCA status. While niraparib is approved across all biomarker subgroups in the CDF, the analysis considers the two BRCA-based populations to align with the decision problem and the relevant comparators specified in the final scope.

A partitioned survival model (PSM) structure was selected with three-health states (Figure 16), including progression-free and alive, progressed and alive, and dead. These states are mutually exclusive and fully exhaustive, meaning that patients must occupy one of the states at any given time. 

A PSM approach was adopted based on the following rationale, which is in line with NICE DSU TSD19 guidance: 

- PSM approaches are generally considered reasonable for advanced or metastatic cancers, as patients tend to have relatively poor survival prognoses and generally cannot return to the original progression-free state. This is consistent with advanced ovarian cancer, where patients with recurrent disease are expected to be incurable. 

- PSMs allow for time-to-event endpoints that are routinely reported in clinical studies for advanced or metastatic cancer treatments (e.g., PFS, OS) to be directly modelled, facilitating easier comparisons for the treatment of interest with external study comparators. 

- Given the use of frequently reported time-to-event endpoints, PSMs are intuitive and simple to communicate and allow relatively close replication of within-trial data. 

- Updated PFS (76.5% event rate – INV assessed PFS) and OS (62.5% event rate) data from the PRIMA trial are relatively mature, with extrapolations of the outcomes therefore expected to provide reasonable representations of the relationship between progression and mortality. 

A PSM approach is also consistent with approaches adopted and accepted in all previous NICE appraisals for 1L PARPi maintenance therapies (TA1055[28] , TA962[70] , TA946[70] , TA693[107] , TA673[26] , TA598[106] ). 

Typical PSMs include three health states (progression-free and alive, progressed and alive, dead). In some instances, a four-state model that further partitions postprogression patients into first and second progression (PFS2) health states has been Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer © GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved Page 130 of 559 



<!-- page 133 -->

adopted. However, the treatment pathway following disease progression with a PARPi monotherapy is the same regardless of the 1L PARPi used, therefore the costs and outcomes resulting from subsequent lines of treatment are expected to be consistent across each treatment sequence. Furthermore, the lack of relevant PFS2 data for comparators outside of the PRIMA trial (i.e. no PFS2 data stratified by low/high risk) has restricted the ability to adequately parametrise relative effectiveness of PFS2 for niraparib vs. active comparators. 

The three-health state model requires survival curves for OS, PFS and TTDD outcomes to estimate the proportions of the model cohort in each of the model states at any point in time. This enables the estimation of treatment costs, disease state costs, and health state utility values to accrue quality-adjusted life years (QALY) and costs over the model time horizon. Visual representations of the three-state approach are shown in Figure 16 and Figure 17. 

Costs, life years (LYs), and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) were accrued over time for each health state and aggregated over the chosen time horizon to calculate the overall health and cost outcomes for each intervention. Depending on the health state and on/off treatment status within the progression-free health state, patients were assigned costs related to drug acquisition, administration, follow-up, monitoring and disease management, and adverse events. Utility values were assigned separately to the progression-free and progressed health states. Overall outcomes depend on the duration of treatment, health state membership, resource use, and associated utilities.

## _**3.3.2.1 Model settings**_ 

In line with the recommendations in the NICE value assessment framework, the CEM adopted an NHS and personal social services (PSS) perspective.[116,117] The model therefore included direct costs relating to drug acquisition and administration, healthcare resource use, adverse event management and end-of-life care. Direct health effects for patients are reported as life years (LYs) and quality-adjusted life 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer © GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved Page 132 of 559 



<!-- page 135 -->

years (QALYs), with health state utility values estimated using the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system and the EQ-5D-3L mapping function recommended in the NICE manual. 

The model considered a ‘lifetime horizon,’ modelling the patient cohort until a negligible proportion remain alive. Since the mean age of patients across the modelled populations of PRIMA trial ranges from xxxx to xxxxx years,[82] the lifetime horizon refers to a time horizon of xxxxx years depending on the analysis population (i.e. up until 100 years of age). A shorter time horizon of 20 years was explored in scenario analysis for both populations. 

A monthly time cycle was applied to the model, aligning with previous NICE Technology Appraisals (TA946[70] , TA962[70] , and TA1055[28] ). Costs, LYs and QALYs accrued are half cycle corrected by taking the average of the values at the start and end of each cycle. However, some cost categories were not subject to half-cycle correction, and these include drug acquisition costs, one-off adverse event costs, and one-off medical resource use costs. Given the relatively short cycle length with respect to the lifetime horizon, it is anticipated that half-cycle correction will have a minimal impact on the model outcomes. 

The annual discount rate for costs and health outcomes was 3.5%, in line with the NICE reference case.[104,117] Alternative discount rates of 1.5% were tested in scenario analysis. 

## **3.3.3 Intervention technology and comparators** 

For the two key populations of interest identified for the submission, the following comparators have been selected: 

## • **For the BRCAm population:** Olaparib; 

## • **For the BRCAwt population** : Rucaparib. 

The current standard of care for BRCAm patients in the UK is olaparib, with rucaparib not currently recommended in the UK for this population. UK clinical experts consulted by GSK indicated that, given the availability of olaparib and the benefits provided by Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer

PARPis in this population, routine surveillance is not considered appropriate a PARPieligible population, and that olaparib is the most relevant comparator for the BRCAm population. 

Rucaparib is currently recommended for both HRd BRCAwt and non-HRD positive populations, which together constitute the BRCAwt population. Although NICE guidance limits the use of rucaparib to bevacizumab-ineligible patients within HRp or HR-unknown patient populations (Section 1.4.3.2), PARPi monotherapies are generally not considered for patients eligible for bevacizumab in the maintenance phase, and therefore this restriction was not considered relevant for this appraisal given current UK clinical practice. The appropriateness of rucaparib as a comparator was also validated by UK clinical experts, who advised rucaparib would be utilised in place of niraparib for BRCAwt patients should niraparib not be routinely available. 

## **3.4 Clinical parameters and variables** 

## **3.4.1 Population characteristics** 

Baseline characteristics of the patient population of interest were informed by pooled arm estimates for each population from the PRIMA trial as outlined in Table 36. Variable body surface area (BSA) was not reported in the trial and therefore it was estimated using the Du Bois formula: BSA = 0.007184*(Height(cm)^0.725)*(Weight(kg)^0.425), where the height and weight at baseline was used. These baseline characteristics were used to calculate weight- or BSA-based dosages. Population-specific eGFR was not available; therefore, for any AUC-based dosing, a mean GFR of 93.0 ml/min/1.73m² was used for all populations, based on the estimate adopted in NICE TA962[27] . Alternative baseline age values, based on median estimates from niraparib SACT data (65 for BRCAm, 70 for BRCAwt), were explored in a scenario analysis.

## **3.4.2 Cure/long-term remission in aOC** 

There is established evidence to support the potential for long-term remission and functional cure (hereafter referred to as “cure”) in 1L aOC maintenance settings. Clinical experts from previous NICE appraisals (TA248, TA962[70] and TA946[70] ) have highlighted the expectation of cure or long-term survival for a small but significant proportion of patients who remain progression-free. This is also supported by longterm data from the literature, which shows ~20% of patients remain progression free and alive after 10 years, with plateauing observed in the PFS curves[3,118] . However, given the broader population included in studies identified from the literature and the focus of the PRIMA trial on high-risk patients, further UK clinical expert feedback was sought to support the long-term remission assumption. 

During an advisory board, UK clinical experts[10] noted that “cure” was possible even in a PRIMA-like population and across all biomarker subgroups based on BRCA or HRD status. Clinical experts highlighted that relapse (i.e. disease progression) typically occurred within the first 5 years of responding to 1L chemotherapy and maintenance treatment, and patients who remained progression-free after 7-10 years were unlikely to relapse. They also generally agreed that long-term remission is not as established in the relapsed setting, with only a small number of patients able to achieve long-term remission. 

Therefore, a user-modifiable cure switch point was incorporated into the economic model, after which patients alive and progression-free (based on PFS) were assumed Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 138 -->

to be “cured” – i.e., remain progression-free and follow the general population mortality thereafter. In line with previous PARPi NICE appraisals, no adjustments were made to the OS extrapolations, which were assumed to continue beyond the cure point until intersecting with the PFS curve, at which point they were capped by the PFS curve from below. This approach leveraged the mature PFS data from PRIMA, which is expected to more accurately reflect the long-term survival plateau associated with the remission assumption. Furthermore, both PFS and OS were capped to ensure that survival rates per cycle did not drop below the (adjusted) general population mortality at any point. Based on the clinical expert feedback received, a 10-year cure timepoint was used in the base case analysis, with both earlier and later cure time points (8 and 12 years) tested in scenario analyses. 

For the BRCAm population, general population mortality applied to PFS after the cure point was adjusted using an HR of 1.26 based on Mai 2009, in line with NICE TA946[70] and TA962[27] , and the impact of excluding this HR estimate was explored in scenario analyses. 

## **3.4.3 Approach to survival analysis and curve selection process** 

PFS and OS survival curves from PRIMA were used to estimate health state membership over time, with TTDD determining the proportion of patients on 1L maintenance treatment over time. Survival curves were extrapolated beyond the observed follow-up period in accordance with NICE DSU guidance.[99,100] . Standard and flexible parametric models were fitted for each biomarker subgroup independently due to the lack of head-to-head comparative trial data between niraparib and olaparib, or with rucaparib. 

**Standard Parametric Models** : Parametric survival models assume that the time-toevent (TTE) outcome follows a parametric distribution. The distributions investigated for PFS, OS, and TTDD included exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log-logistic, lognormal, gamma, and generalised gamma distributions. 

**Flexible Parametric Spline Models** : an alternative flexible spline modelling approach was explored for PFS and OS, considering that standard parametric models might not necessarily provide reasonable fits to the PRIMA time-to-event data given the Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 139 -->

flattening of the observed KM data. Based on recent guidance on alternative parametric models[119] and their use in recent PARPi CDF exit appraisals, Royston/Parmar flexible spline models were investigated considering all three spline model types (hazards, odds, normal) and 1-3 internal knots.[120] 

While mixture cure models (MCMs) were also considered, flexible parametric spline models were considered preferable, as UK health economic experts consulted by GSK[10] highlighted that splines are likely to produce comparable extrapolations to MCMs when mature survival data is available. Furthermore, MCMs pose several implementational challenges, particularly when linking cure fractions across outcomes, as proposed in TA962. This approach requires fitting numerous OS parametric models for each PFS cure fraction, leading to an impractically large number of models to evaluate. Further details on the curve selection process and rationale for model selection are provided in Appendix J. Extrapolations selected for the base case and scenario analyses are summarised in the subsequent sections.

## **3.4.6 PFS and OS: Modelling of external comparators** 

There are no direct comparisons between niraparib and the relevant comparators (olaparib and rucaparib) in a clinical trial setting in 1L aOC maintenance. Therefore, an ITC feasibility assessment was conducted, which concluded that any ITCs involving comparison of niraparib (PRIMA, PRIME) trials vs. olaparib (SOLO-1) and rucaparib (ATHENA-MONO) trials are likely inappropriate and fundamentally flawed, as described in Section 2.7.

<!-- page 146 -->

Despite the significant limitations identified in the ITC FA, several exploratory ITCs were conducted, to obtain relative treatment effects across different outcomes and treatments and within each population of interest (see Section 2.7). 

The exploratory ITC using PRIMA and SOLO-1 indicated no statistically significant differences in PFS outcomes for niraparib compared to olaparib in the BRCAm population. While the unadjusted Bucher ITC nominally favoured olaparib, the result was not statistically significant (xx xxxx xxx x xxxx xxxxx x xxxx]), and numerical differences were likely due to differences in the PRIMA and SOLO-1 trial design and populations. Furthermore, the absence of detailed patient characteristics for the highrisk BRCAm population subgroup of SOLO-1 (including key prognostic factors such as NVRD status) made it impossible to rule out potential imbalances in effect modifiers between studies that would impact the results of an unadjusted analysis. As noted in Section 2.7, population-adjusted methods (STC) were initially considered but the regression model lacked external validity. 

Exploratory ITCs for niraparib versus rucaparib using PRIME and ATHENA-MONO (Section 2.7), in the absence of high-risk data for rucaparib, also indicated no statistically significant differences in PFS across all populations and for OS for the ITT and HRd populations (other subpopulation specific OS data was not available from PRIME). 

In the absence of OS outcomes for high-risk patients from SOLO-1, OS data for BRCAm patients receiving olaparib and niraparib from the SACT was reviewed, to assess whether survival differences between niraparib and olaparib survival could be expected. As shown in Figure 22, the SACT OS KM curves for niraparib and olaparib overlap for the first 27 months, before only deviating slightly at the tails where low numbers of patients at risk are available to inform the niraparib curve. Furthermore, the proportion of patients alive at key SACT milestones (6-24 months) is similar between niraparib and olaparib, as summarised in Table 39.

Real-world evidence studies comparing PARPis effectiveness in 1L aOC maintenance are currently limited, thus restricting the use of RWE comparative effectiveness for the CEM (Section 2.8.1). Nevertheless, equivalence in niraparib and olaparib efficacy is supported by a recent real-world evidence study[96] (South Korea) in BRCAm patients, where similar outcomes between olaparib and niraparib when used as maintenance therapy were demonstrated, with no statistically significant differences in PFS (HR: 1.08; 95% CI: 0.47, 2.52; p=0.854), TFST (HR: 1.20; 95% CI: 0.51, 2.81; p=0.682) or OS (HR: 0.42; 95% CI: 0.01, 17.61; p=0.649 – note that only 2 deaths were observed in the olaparib arm and none in the niraparib arm). 

Clinical expert feedback also supports the expectation of a class effect for PARPis, with no meaningful differences in efficacy across the approved drugs. This ‘class effect’ is more evident in the relapsed setting where pivotal trials of PARPi treatments are more comparable.[21-23] Experts highlighted that the alignment between UK SACT OS data for niraparib and olaparib, along with supportive findings from the above mentioned South Korean study[96] , provides valuable evidence of this class effect. Experts also noted that PFS and OS outcomes for niraparib from PRIMA and rucaparib from ATHENA-MONO[28] were also considered comparable, despite differences in study design and patient characteristics, with no clinically meaningful differences between hazard ratios across biomarker populations. However, experts acknowledge that interpreting OS data, particularly for some subgroups, was more challenging due to differences in data maturity between the two studies.

## **3.4.7 TTDD** 

## **Niraparib** 

Although the niraparib SmPC does not specify a maximum duration of treatment, both PRIMA and PRIME trial protocols specified a 36-month stopping rule, which is typically adhered to by clinicians in UK clinical practice. While some patients in the trial continued niraparib beyond this period, feedback from UK clinical experts during an advisory board suggested that only a very small proportion of patients in UK clinical practice would be expected to continue treatment beyond 36 months. This is primarily due to risk benefit ratio as there is a lack of clinical trial evidence demonstrating the efficacy and safety beyond 3 years and concerns regarding cumulative toxicity and the associated risks of AML and MDS with prolonged PARPi use. As a result, continued treatment with PARPi is likely to be limited to patients with visible disease who remain progression-free and continue to respond to treatment after three years. Clinical experts also noted that discontinuing niraparib after 36 months is unlikely to impact efficacy outcomes. 

According to clinical experts, the proportion of patients remaining on niraparib treatment after 36 months is estimated to range from 5% to 10%, influenced by factors such as surgical outcomes and the extent of residual disease, which can vary across 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 150 -->

regions due to differences in healthcare practices and access to care prior to initiating and during PARPi treatment. 

Therefore, in the base case scenario, it was assumed that 90% of patients will discontinue niraparib after 36 months, while 10% will remain on treatment. Those remaining beyond the stopping rule are assumed to follow the same TTDD curve projection as applied prior to the stopping rule. 

For the base case analysis, PRIMA TTDD data were utilised to align with use of PRIMA data for PFS and OS in the model. Given the limited need to extrapolate TTDD beyond the observed data based on clinical expert feedback, the statistical and visual fit of parametric models for niraparib TTDD were used as the primary selection criteria, in line with NICE DSU TSD14 guidance[99] . However, as none of the models demonstrated particularly strong visual fits to the observed data (Appendix J: Clinical Inputs: Survival Analysis), TTDD was modelled using the available KM data from PRIMA combined with the parametric model that provided the best statistical fit for each population (exponential for BRCAm, log-logistic for BRCAwt) to extrapolate beyond the observed data. 

## **- Comparators olaparib and rucaparib** 

For external comparators, published TTDD KM curves were available for olaparib from SOLO-1 and SACT data; however, comparable TTDD curves were not available for rucaparib. Median time on treatment estimates were available from both SOLO-1 for olaparib (24.6 months) and ATHENA-MONO for rucaparib (14.7 months). However, median treatment duration data were available only for the overall population from ATHENA-MONO, which is likely to overestimate time on treatment for a BRCAwt population. 

To ensure a consistent approach across PARPi comparators and to produce a more conservative estimate for rucaparib, TTDD curves were instead generated by adjusting the base case PFS curves for each treatment arm with AE discontinuation probabilities. For olaparib in the BRCAm population, a constant AE discontinuation rate was estimated based on the probability of AE-related discontinuation (11.92%)

<!-- page 151 -->

and the median treatment exposure (24.6 months) from SOLO-1.[17] Similarly, for rucaparib in the BRCAwt population, a constant AE discontinuation rate was calculated based on the probability of AE-related discontinuation (11.76%) and the median treatment exposure (14.7 months) from ATHENA-MONO.[14] 

SOLO-1[17] and olaparib SACT data showed that some patients continued treatment beyond 24 months. However, as cumulative toxicity and the associated risks of AML and MDS with prolonged PARPi use are class-wide concerns, the assumption that 10% of patients would continue treatment beyond the stopping rule for niraparib was also applied to olaparib and rucaparib in the base-case analyses for the BRCAm and BRCAwt populations, respectively. However, this assumption may underestimate the true costs of olaparib and rucaparib as clinical experts noted that in clinical practice there was greater scope for continuing treatment beyond the stopping rule for these therapies (relative to niraparib) as the overall exposure is shorter; suggesting that the proportion continuing on olaparib or rucaparib is likely to be higher due to the earlier treatment stopping rule at 24 months.

## **3.4.9 Treatment waning** 

Treatment effect waning was not considered relevant across any of the 1L PARPi CDF exit appraisals for olaparib + bevacizumab (TA946[70] ), olaparib (TA962[27] ) or rucaparib (TA1055[28] ), or across identified model publications reviewed. Omission of waning is consistent with the clinical intent of PARPi, which is to maintain remission beyond the first 2-3 years following PBC when the risk of relapse is greatest. Patients who remain progression-free beyond this period are considered to be at low risk of progression. Therefore, incorporating treatment waning following discontinuation of PARPi in survival modelling was not considered appropriate. 

## **3.4.10 Adverse events** 

In the CEM, grade 3 or above treatment-related AEs that occurred in more than 5% of patients in either arm of each study were considered to capture impact on costs and health-related quality of life (HRQoL), in alignment with the approach previously adopted for niraparib in NICE TA 673.[26] The impact of AEs on healthcare resource utilisation costs, and HRQoL were captured as one-off costs and one-off QALY loss at treatment initiation (i.e., in the first modelled cycle), respectively, as in previous NICE TAs (TA946[70] , TA962[27] , TA1055[28] ). While AEs can occur at any point during 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 155 -->

treatment, they are assumed to occur primarily after treatment initiation and require only acute care. 

AE probabilities for niraparib were extracted from both the PRIMA trial and from the MONITOR-UK study[75] , while those for the comparators olaparib and rucaparib were obtained from their respective pivotal trials (Table 42). For the base case analysis, MONITOR-UK data were used for niraparib as the starting dose distribution (16% on 300mg, 79% on 200mg, 5% on 100mg) was more reflective of UK clinical practice, and also more comparable to the SACT data used to model the niraparib dose distribution in the base case analysis (see Section 3.6.1). This approach was validated during one-to-one follow-up interviews with three UK clinical experts, who confirmed that the AE frequencies observed in MONITOR-UK were appropriate and more reflective of niraparib use in UK clinical practice. 

Although phase 3 trial data were used to model AEs for olaparib and rucaparib, realworld evidence for olaparib[121] suggests that its AE profile is fairly similar to that observed in SOLO-1. In contrast, the differences observed between AEs in the realworld and PRIMA could be attributed largely to a greater proportion of patients starting on the 300 mg dose which is associated with higher rates of AEs and lower tolerability. Additionally, niraparib is the only PARPi treatment where the marketing authorisation mandates weekly blood count tests for the first month of treatment followed by monthly tests for the following 9 months. Clinicians noted that AEs are generally lower at the 200 mg dose; individualised dosing schedule combined with proactive monitoring and pre-emptive AE management, helps reduce the incidence of serious AEs. A GSK sponsored patient support program is in place which provides blood testing and blood pressure monitoring services at home to patients being treated with niraparib. This minimises patient barriers to testing services which are required by the SmPC and serves to proactively manage incidences of adverse effects. 

AE data for PARPi’s was also assumed to be consistent across population subgroups. This approach is consistent with previous TAs (TA946[70] , TA962[27] , TA1055[28] ). Application of PRIMA AE estimates was explored in scenario analysis.

## **3.5 Measurement and valuation of health effects** 

## **3.5.1 Health-related quality-of-life data from clinical trials** 

In PRIMA, patient HRQoL was a secondary end point and was assessed using the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer [EORTC] Quality of Life Questionnaire [EORTC QLQ-C30], the EORTC Quality of Life Questionnaire Ovarian Cancer module [EORTC QLQ-OV28]), the FOSI, and the EQ-5D-5L.[69] A statistical analysis of HRQoL data from PRIMA conducted by GSK was used to capture HRQoL differences between progression-free and progressed patients (progression effects). EQ-5D-5L response data from PRIMA were converted to EQ5D-3L scores using the Hernandez-Alava 2020 cross-walk algorithm in line with NICE recommendations.[104,117] 

Potential differences in HRQoL were assessed using a generalised estimating equation (GEE) model with an identity link function, with various GEE models explored including progression, treatment arm and population subgroup as covariates. However, given the lack of significant differences in health state specific utilities by treatment arm and population subgroup, and in line with prior NICE appraisals, the same set of utility estimates derived from the overall PRIMA trial population were considered for both BRCAm and BRCAwt populations. 

## **3.5.2 Mapping** 

As per NICE guidance [50], EQ-5D-5L response data from PRIMA were converted to EQ-5D-3L scores using the Hernandez-Alava 2020 cross-walk algorithm, as stated in Section 3.4.1. No other mapping was performed. 

## **3.5.3 Health-related quality-of-life studies** 

The clinical SLR identified four studies evaluating 1L PARPi maintenance treatments with relevant HRQoL data. These studies relate to the RCTs for niraparib[12] , rucaparib[14] , olaparib[15] and olaparib plus bevacizumab[64] main clinical trial publications. Data on EORTC QLQ-C30 and EQ-5D were available from two RCTs each (PAOLA1 and PRIMA, and SOLO-1 and PRIMA, respectively). To note that in both PRIMA (niraparib) and SOLO-1 (olaparib), similar EQ-5D-5L scores were seen regardless of

Utility values were applied to each health state in the model (progression free and progressed) to capture patient QoL associated with treatment and disease outcomes and were assumed to be the same regardless of the treatment (i.e., utility values are assumed to remain unchanged regardless of treatment arms). This assumption is in line with clinical advice to the EAG in TA1055[28] , which highlighted that HRQoL is not likely to differ by subgroups. 

Utility values in the model are adjusted by age to reflect decreases in HRQoL over time using a multiplicative approach[123] (NICE guidance 4.3.7[104,117] ). In line with NICE guidance, these adjustments were made to account for the expected decline in QoL associated with age and to prevent health state utilities exceeding those of the agematched UK general population. UK general population utility norms were sourced from the Hernandez-Alava 2022 NICE DSU report, where general population utility was derived from an adjusted limited dependent variable mixture model (ALDVMM) fitted to UK Health Survey for England EQ-5D-3L data.[17]

## **3.6 Cost and healthcare resource use identification, measurement and valuation** 

Thirteen studies were identified for the SLR that reported on HCRU/costs, including the three NICE technology appraisals previously reviewed (TA962[27] , TA946[70] and TA1055[28] ). Search terms are summarised in Appendix G:. Full details on the findings of the HCRU/costs SLR including PRISMA diagram and outcomes are detailed in Appendix G:. Given their recency and use of a UK NHS and PSS payer perspective, the recent three prior PARPi NICE technology appraisals were considered most relevant for informing cost category inclusion and sourcing of cost inputs compared to other publications identified.

<!-- page 162 -->

Based on review of published economic studies and prior NICE appraisals, the model included the following cost categories: drug acquisition and administration, adverse event management, follow-up and monitoring, terminal care and subsequent treatment costs. The following sections describe the assumptions and the inputs used for each cost category included in the model. 

## **3.6.1 Intervention and comparators’ costs and resource use** 

## _**Drug Acquisition Costs**_ 

Drug acquisition costs for each treatment regimen were calculated based on cost per package and dosing regimen (including dose per administration and number of administrations) reported in the respective prescribing information and/or clinical trials. Unit cost per package was obtained from (i) latest data from British National Formulary and (ii) the latest drugs and pharmaceutical electronic market information tool (eMIT).[116,124] 

If multiple formulations of a treatment with similar strength were available, an average cost was calculated for use in the model. For treatments with multiple formulations with different strengths, the least expensive formulation that aligns with the prescribed dosing was selected.

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 163 -->

Niraparib is an oral monotherapy with a recommended starting dose of 200 mg (two 100 mg capsules), taken once daily (OD). For patients who weigh ≥ 77 kg and have baseline platelet count ≥ 150,000/μL, the recommended starting dose of niraparib is 300 mg OD (three 100 mg capsules). In the base case analysis, the modeling approach for niraparib dosing considered the proportion of patients starting on 200 mg versus 300 mg and incorporated the relative dose intensity for patients starting on each dose. The distribution of patients starting on 200mg or 300mg, as provided by the SACT data was seen as the most accurate reflection of UK clinical practice and is also aligned with available dose distribution data from the MONITOR-UK study[25] which clinical experts stated was a more accurate reflection of niraparib use in UK clinical practice. 

Relative dose intensity (RDI) was considered to account for the impact that dose modifications have on drug costs, with niraparib RDI estimates sourced from PRIMA in the absence of available information from other data sources. RDI for niraparib is expected to be lower as patients tend to get down dosed frequently as observed in RWE (such as MONITOR-UK[25] and Bruno et al.[97] ), which was also noted by UK clinical experts (see Section 3.4.10). 

RDI is particularly relevant for niraparib due to its linear pricing structure, distinguishing it from olaparib and rucaparib. While dose reductions are observed across all PARPis, cost savings are only realised with niraparib. Niraparib is formulated as 100 mg tablets which are used to make up daily doses of 100 mg, 200 mg or 300mg per day. In this regard niraparib is linearly priced, with the monthly cost per patient dependent on the average dose received within that month. Conversely, rucaparib is formulated as a 300 mg, 250 mg or 200 mg tablet, each packaged as a 60-tablet pack with the same cost-per-pack as outlined in Table 48. Therefore, dose adjustments which result in a dose reduction from the recommended starting dose of 600 mg per day down to 500 mg or 400 mg per day do not impact on the average daily cost. Similarly in the case of olaparib, 56-tablet packs of 150 mg and 100 mg tablet packs are also flat priced meaning dose adjustments will not impact on the average monthly cost. Furthermore, unlike in the case of niraparib, dose adjustments for rucaparib and olaparib, particularly those occurring mid-cycle, are likely to result in wastage and increased Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 164 -->

monthly costs. Unused tablets from discontinued pack strengths are discarded, requiring patients to switch to a lower pack strength. Data on mid-cycle dose adjustments are not available for olaparib and rucaparib and so are conservatively not accounted for in the cost-effectiveness analysis. Given this, RDI parameters were not applied for olaparib and rucaparib in the base case analyses, with RDIs for olaparib (96.0%) and rucaparib (88.0%) applied in NICE TA1055 explored in scenario analysis for the BRCAm and BRCAwt populations, respectively.

## **3.6.2 Health-state unit costs and resource use** 

Based on previous NICE TA economic evaluations[27,28,70] and clinical expert feedback, follow-up and monitoring cost consists of outpatient oncologist consultation, laboratory tests for complete blood count and imaging procedures (CT-scan). Resource utilisation was modelled separately for the following health states. 

- Progression-free - On maintenance treatment 

- Progression-free - Off maintenance treatment 

- Progressed disease 

Annual frequency of resources incurred in the above-mentioned health states can be stratified by treatment in the model. In the absence of available data to differentiate 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 167 -->

monitoring frequencies by treatment within health states, the same health-state specific frequencies were generally applied to all treatments, with two exceptions. The model allows for additional one-off monitoring costs in the first cycle, which was applied for niraparib to account for additional blood tests required in the first cycle, calculated as 2.67 completed blood tests to produce 4 total blood tests when combined with the monthly frequency of 1.33 blood tests applied in the progression-free on treatment health state, as per UK SMPC.[24] 

In line with NICE TA962[27] and TA946[70] , a 7-year stopping rule was applied in the base case, meaning patients no longer incur resource use costs in the progression-free ontreatment health state after this time point. A scenario analysis was also conducted where no stopping rule was applied to progression-free on-treatment health state resource use.

## **3.6.4 Subsequent treatment costs** 

A proportion of patients that experience progression are expected to receive additional drug-based interventions, including platinum- and non-platinum chemotherapy regimens. Although PARPi use in subsequent treatment lines was observed in the intervention arms across the relevant PRAPi trial, including PRIMA, PARPi re- 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 170 -->

treatment is not allowed in UK clinical practice, as noted in prior PARPi NICE appraisals (TA962[27] , TA946[70] and TA1055[28] ), with clinical experts in TA962[27] indicating the lack of evidence to support the efficacy of PARPi re-treatment. This assumption was also validated with UK clinical experts at one-to-one interviews, with clinical experts noting the lack of clinically meaningful improvement when PARPi’s are given in subsequent lines.[127] This assumption was also validated with UK clinical experts at one-to-one interviews, with clinical experts noting the lack of clinically meaningful improvement when PARPi’s are given in subsequent lines.[127] 

In the model, distributions and durations of subsequent treatments are differentiated between second-line and third-line plus treatment to help to reflect potential differences in subsequent treatment based on the line of therapy. Subsequent treatment costs were applied to the estimated incidence of progression based on the per-cycle change of the progression health state adjusted for mortality (i.e. accounting for the proportion of patients from the previous cycle that would die based on per-cycle OS risk). 

The proportion of patients receiving each subsequent treatment upon progression with a PARPi is derived from treatment usage observed within the PRIMA trial. Subsequent treatment distributions applied in the model were derived in several stages: 

- The proportions applied in the model were calculated as percentages of the total niraparib patients with a first progression event (n=xx for BRCAm, n=xxx for BRCAwt) for 2L subsequent treatments and of patients with a second progression event (n=xx for BRCAm, n=xxx for BRCAwt) for 3L+ subsequent treatments in PRIMA. 

- Given that PARPi retreatment and bevacizumab are not permitted as subsequent line treatments in NHS practice, but are recorded as subsequent treatment in the PRIMA trial, the proportion of patients receiving these treatments are redistributed proportionally to each of the other chemotherapy agents. These proportions were validated with UK clinicians who confirmed them to representative of subsequent treatments used in clinical practice. 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 171 -->

- 3L+ treatment distributions were also multiplied by the proportion of first progression patients in PRIMA who also reported experiencing a PFS2 event, i.e. a second relapse, calculated as xxxx% of the BRCAm population and xxxx% of the BRCAwt population.

## _**Terminal Care Costs**_ 

In line with NICE TA946[70] and TA962[27] , patients incur a one-off terminal care cost applied at the time of death, with the same estimate applied to all death events. The unit cost was derived from recent nice appraisals (NICE TA946[70] and TA962[27] ) which used an estimate from Guest et al. [2006][128] using the £8,053.63 estimate from those appraisals and inflated from 2021 to 2024 costs based on PSSRU inflation indices. Also in line with NICE TA946[70] and TA962[27] , the model assumes that 51.28% of patients will receive end-of-life care based on data from a UK study by Gao et a. 2013.[129] Due to a lack of identified uncertainty data, SEs are assumed equal to 10% of the mean value.

## **3.11 Exploring uncertainty** 

This section will provide a comprehensive assessment of uncertainty, examining the relative impact of various types of uncertainty on cost-effectiveness estimates. It will evaluate whether any potential uncertainties around modelling assumptions included in the analyses have been adequately captured and will identify any uncertainties that are unlikely to be mitigated by additional evidence or expert input. 

## **3.11.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

PSA was conducted to assess the parameter uncertainty and mean PSA result was used as the base case. All key parameters were assigned probability distributions and point estimates were drawn using Monte Carlo simulation techniques. The PSA was run for 5,000 iterations as this was found to be sufficient to produce stable results. Results from the PSA for both the BRCAm (vs. olaparib) and BRCAwt (vs. rucaparib) population base-case analyses are presented in Table 64 and Table 65, using the PAS price for niraparib. The results demonstrate good consistency with the deterministic analysis and show that niraparib remains a cost-effective treatment strategy versus olaparib and rucaparib, resulting in cost savings. 

The cost-effectiveness plane for niraparib versus olaparib and versus rucaparib is presented in xxxxxx 26 and xxxxxx 27, respectively. At a willingness to pay threshold of £30,000, niraparib has a 100% probability of being cost-effective compared with olaparib and rucaparib. The cost-effectiveness acceptability curves of niraparib versus olaparib and versus rucaparib are not presented, since niraparib is cost-effective with 100% probability up to very large willingness to pay thresholds.
