## **3.12 Subgroup analysis** 

No other subgroup analyses were conducted for the submission. 

## **3.13 Benefits not captured in the QALY calculation** 

Having more than a single treatment available to help delay disease progression in 1L OC maintenance is essential for optimizing patient care and maximising population health. Such benefits are poorly captured within conventional cost-utility analysis. Every individual responds differently to medications due to factors such as genetics, age, lifestyle, comorbidities, and disease progression. Offering a variety of treatments enables healthcare providers to tailor therapies to meet the unique needs of each patient, enhancing efficacy, minimizing adverse effects and improving health outcomes overall. Furthermore, the availability of diverse treatments fosters innovation, encourages competition, and drives continual improvement in therapeutic approaches, ultimately improving health outcomes and ensuring that more patients can access effective care suited to their circumstances. 

## **3.14 Validation** 

Technical validation process leveraged external published validation guidelines[132] to ensure the model was implemented accurately. 

The validation process was conducted in three main steps. At the end of draft model implementation, the project team conducted the following standardised checks to identify implementation issues and ensure that the model is ready for technical verification by an experienced team member that was not involved in the project. Unexpected model behaviours after each step was examined to ensure that it stems from the model design and not from implementation error, with any inconsistencies or identified issues recorded and corrected. 

- Step 1A - Functionality testing (FT). A procedure for testing a model during which all key buttons (e.g. buttons to run a simulation, buttons to run sensitivity analyses) and toggles (e.g. dropdowns) are clicked or switched and the impact on the model interface, outcomes, or both is evaluated. 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 190 -->

- Step 1B - Extreme value testing (EVT). A procedure for testing a model during which all key model inputs (e.g. efficacy, safety, costs, utility) are varied to low and high extreme values (determined on a case by case basis by parameter type) with the impact evaluated on the direct outcomes (e.g. high/low values for drug unit cost evaluated on total drug cost predicted by the model) 

- Step 1C – Scenario/Logic check testing.  A procedure for testing a model during which a pre-defined list of scenarios/logic checks is set up in the model and the scenario/logic checks results compared with the expected outcomes (i.e. model outcomes of each scenario/logic check should align with a priori expectations). 

Technical verification (Step 2) was then performed by an internal peer reviewer not involved with the original programming. This technical validation reviewed the interface, parameters, calculations, engine, results sheet, DSA, PSA, and any other ancillary code (e.g. VBA). Unexpected model behaviour, implementation, and typing errors identified by this review was updated in the model and resolved. 

In addition, a team member independent to the project team reviewed the extracted model inputs (Step 3A), to verify the accuracy of data input extraction by comparison of values to original data sources (including transformations of parameters to derive model inputs are correctly calculated - e.g. rate to probability conversions). Furthermore, internal predictive validation (Step 3B) was conducted (e.g. comparison of survival analyses predictions calculated in the economic model vs. statistical report outputs and observed data from the original study), with any identified discrepancies addressed. 

Once technical validation was completed, discussion with UK clinical and health economic experts was also conducted to help validate key model assumptions (e.g. cure plausibility, parametric survival model approach) and conduct predictive validation of long-term survival extrapolations for niraparib. An advisory board was conducted with three UK clinical experts and two UK health economic modelling experts. A one-to-one interview with an additional clinical expert not included in the advisory board was undertaken, along with three further one-to-one interviews with Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 191 -->

each of the UK clinical experts included in the advisory board.  A one-to-one interview with an additional UK health economics expert (not involved in the advisory board) was also conducted. 

## **3.15 Interpretation and conclusions of economic evidence** 

A _de novo_ cost-utility model was developed to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of niraparib compared to relevant comparators as maintenance treatment in women with newly diagnosed advanced OC. This evaluation considered two patient populations of interest according to their BRCA status: patients with a BRCA mutation and patients without a BRCA mutation, BRCAwt. This bespoke evaluation by (sub-)population reflects both differences in treatment options and differences in prognosis. 

In the BRCAm population, and compared to olaparib, the cost-effectiveness deterministic base-case results indicated that niraparib may be cost saving (xxxxxxxx with the PAS price for niraparib) and equivalent, with a minor non-clinically relevant QALY difference (incremental QALY of xxxxxxx). The estimated incremental net monetary benefit at a £30,000 per QALY gained cost-effectiveness threshold is xxxxxxx, with similar estimate when using a £20,000 per QALY gained threshold value. In patients with BRCAwt, niraparib is considered cost-effective compared to rucaparib with cost savings amounting to £xxxxxx with niraparib PAS price, and marginal difference in incremental QALYs (of xxxxxxx). Thus, niraparib is less costly than rucaparib, at almost equivalent QALYs. However, these estimates do not take into account any confidential net price discounts. 

Probabilistic base-case results are closely aligned with the deterministic base-case results outlined. Considering that different decision rules are applicable to both populations as simulations fall on different quadrants of the cost-effectiveness plane, the probability of niraparib being cost-effective in both populations is 100% across a range of cost-effectiveness thresholds (from £0 to £350,000). 

For both the BRCAm and BRCAwt populations, the results of one-way deterministic sensitivity analyses indicated that results are robust to changes in key economic model parameters. 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 192 -->

Given the results obtained, niraparib can be considered a cost-effective treatment option regardless of a patient’s BRCA status in the 1L maintenance setting, where patients still have limited treatment options, i.e. olaparib for mutated and rucaparib for non-mutated. 

The main strengths of the economic analysis performed are: 

- Niraparib’s efficacy data is primarily sourced from the PRIMA trial, a high-quality multicentre phase III randomised trial of patients with advanced stage III-IV ovarian cancer. PRIMA included UK patients with aOC, enhancing its representativeness of 1L aOC UK patients. The maturity of the PRIMA trial survival data is considered high at 76.5% for PFS and 62.5% for OS. 

- The economic model has been populated by randomised trial data but also informed by relevant published literature and leveraged UK real world evidence. 

- Survival outcomes predictions and key modelling assumptions have been thoroughly validated by UK clinical expert opinion, reflecting the most up to date UK clinical practice. 

- Health state utility values, independent of treatment, were derived from the PRIMA trial, which is the most relevant evidence to inform the health-related quality of life of these populations. 

- All health care resource consumption and costs used in the economic model have been sourced from UK published sources, with inflation to 2024 prices where needed. Health care resource use estimates were validated by UK clinical experts. 

The main limitations of the economic analysis performed are: 

- No direct head-to-head evidence is available to inform the comparative effectiveness between niraparib and the relevant PARPi comparators. In addition, available data does not allow for robust, adjusted, indirect comparisons. However, PARPi equivalence is supported by results of 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 193 -->

exploratory ITC analysis (Section 2.7), RWE and UK clinical expert opinion. Scenario analysis explored alternatives to the base case assumptions. 

- Economic model requirements implied that clinical benefits beyond the duration of the PRIMA trial were estimated through the fitting of standard and flexible parametric distributions to patient level survival data to estimate long-term PFS, OS, and TTDD. Although PRIMA trial survival data is considered mature, survival modelling assumptions inherently imply some level of uncertainty. The methods for survival extrapolation followed the NICE DSU guidelines and the survival extrapolations were validated by UK clinical experts. Alternative parametric survival distributions (pessimistic and optimistic) were evaluated in scenario analysis, although, given the equivalence of PFS and OS between niraparib and comparator treatments, these are unlikely to be a driver of economic model results. 

- Given evidence from relevant published literature, previous appraisals and UK clinical expert opinion, in the economic model it was assumed that if patients remained progression-free for 10 years, long-term remission is considered. Thus, although uncertain, in the base case analysis a PFS cure landmark was considered at 10 years. Early and later cure points were evaluated in scenario analysis but with no significant impact on base case results. 

- TTDD data for niraparib from PRIMA was complemented by UK clinical expert opinion and RWE to inform assumptions regarding the proportion of patients who remained on niraparib treatment post-36 months. In the absence of TTDD KM data for the comparator therapies from their pivotal trials, these were estimated based on PFS and AE-related discontinuation in the base case. Uncertainty in TTDD was explored through scenario analysis and did not substantially affect interpretation of the base case cost-effectiveness results for either population. 

Results indicate that niraparib is a cost-effective option compared to olaparib and rucaparib in the BRCAm and BRCAwt populations, respectively.

## **Appendix B: Identification, selection and synthesis of clinical evidence** 

## **B1.1 Identification and selection of relevant studies** 

An SLR was conducted in March 2024, with an update in February 2025, to identify evidence on the efficacy, safety and HRQoL of niraparib and relevant comparators in adults with advanced epithelial (FIGO stages III and IV) high-grade ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer, who have not progressed following first-line therapy, based on data from clinical trials and real-world evidence studies.[20] Studies were identified using a search strategy to search across relevant platforms (via the Ovid platform as well as conference proceedings and HTA websites). Inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied to studies to determine those most relevant for inclusion in this submission.[20] 

## **B.1.1.1 Search strategy** 

The 2024 SLR and the 2025 update were conducted based on the reporting standards of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA), general methodological requirements outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and key HTA bodies, such as NICE.[20] 

The literature database searches included a combination of free-text and controlled vocabulary terms specific to each database.[20] The search strategy included terms for ovarian cancer which were combined with first-line and maintenance terms.[20] Terms specific to interventions of interest (e.g., PARPis, bevacizumab and monitoring) were added to focus the search strategy on relevant comparators of interest, which include those currently approved, recommended in clinical guidelines or a future comparator for PRIMA.[20] 

The SLR included full-text, peer-reviewed articles and evidence from pre-defined grey literature sources[20] The following databases were searched via the Ovid platform:[20] 

- MEDLINE and MEDLINE In-process 

- Embase 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer

<!-- page 212 -->

- EBM Reviews: Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) 

- NHS EED (via CRD) 

- NHS HTA (via CRD) 

Relevant abstracts from conference proceedings not indexed in Embase were manually searched using the conference website (2020-current):[20] 

- European Society of Gynaecological Oncology (ESGO) 

- American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) 

- European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO): annual meeting; Asia congress; gynaecological cancers congress and Targeted Anticancer Therapies 

- Asian Society of Gynaecologic Oncology (ASGO) 

- Society of Gynaecologic Oncology (SGO) 

- National Cancer Research Institute (NCRI) 

- European Association for Cancer Research (EACR) 

- The Professional Society for Health Economics and Outcomes Research (ISPOR): annual meeting; Europe annual; Asia Pacific 

- International Gynaecologic Cancer Society (IGCS) 

- British Gynaecological Cancer Society (BGCS) 

To identify any clinical data not otherwise available in peer-reviewed journals or conference abstracts, a search of prior HTA submissions was conducted, including:[20] 

- NICE 

- Scottish Medicines Consortium (SMC) 

- National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics (NCPE) 

- Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health (CADTH)/pan-Canadian Oncology Drug Review (pCODR) 

- Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee (PBAC)

The screening was conducted in two phases using PICOs criteria (as specified in Table 82): a) title/abstract screening, and b) full-text screening. At each phase, all records were screened by two independent reviewers, with conflicts resolved by a third independent reviewer.[20] Following the article selection process, a preliminary list of included and excluded studies (with reasons for exclusion at the full-text screening level) was generated.[20] 

## **B.1.1.3 Data extraction and quality assessment** 

Data from the included studies was extracted into standardised data extraction templates developed in Microsoft Excel[®] with separate tabs to capture publication, study, patient, and treatment characteristics, as well as outcome data of interest.[20] The data was extracted by one reviewer and a second reviewer assessed the entries to ensure consistency and accuracy.[20] 

A quality assessment of the primary, full-text studies was conducted using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Assessment Tool 2.0 for RCTs,[133] as recommended by HTA Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 229 -->

bodies, such as NICE. RWE studies and single-arm trials were assessed using the Risk of Bias in Non-Randomised Studies – of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool.[134] Conference abstracts were not quality assessed, given the limited information provided. 

## **B.1.1.4 Results** 

## _**Overview of search results**_ 

The original SLR was conducted in March 2024 and resulted in the inclusion of 117 publications representing 31 unique studies.[20] An update was conducted in February 2025 and yielded 653 records.[20] Of 507 unique records screened at the title and abstract level that remained after removing 146 duplicates, 149 were deemed eligible for full-text screening, while the others were excluded.[20] After the full-text review, a total of 33 records were included for synthesis from the database searches, and 1 record was additionally included from grey literature searches.[20] Therefore, a total of 34 records for 14 unique studies were included in the 2025 SLR update.[20] 

Accounting for the original SLR and subsequent updates, a total of 151 publications were included, representing 45 unique studies, including 8 clinical trials and 37 RWE studies.[20] Figure 30 shows the PRISMA diagram for the 2024 SLR and 2025 SLR update.

## **B.1.1.5 Summary of trials used for indirect or mixed treatment comparisons** 

The clinical SLR identified eight relevant studies for 1L maintenance in aOC: SOLO1, PAOLA-1, ATHENA-MONO, PRIME, PRIMA, FLAMES, OVARIO, Oda 2024 (Appendix B.1.1.4).[20] The Oda 2024 trial was excluded on the basis that it was a Phase 2 single-arm trial with limited sample size (N=32), while the FLAMES, 

OVARIO and PAOLA-1 trials were excluded as they assessed seneparib, niraparib plus bevacizumab and olaparib plus bevacizumab as interventions, respectively, which are not considered relevant comparators for niraparib.[20] The PARPi 

monotherapy treatment options (olaparib and rucaparib) which are considered relevant comparators for niraparib are listed in Section 1.2, along with the rationale for their relevance. 

## _**Methods and outcomes of studies included in indirect or mixed treatment comparisons**_ 

Four unique clinical trials were identified and included in the ITC feasibility assessment (FA). Only studies assessing PARPi monotherapy initiated during the maintenance phase were included in the assessment (Section 2.7, Figure 10). The primary focus was to determine the possibility of estimating relative effects for olaparib vs niraparib in the BRCAm and high-risk subgroup and rucaparib vs niraparib in the BRCAwt subgroup.

## **Study Design** 

All four RCTs included in the ITC FA were generally similar in terms of study design (i.e., phase 3 and double-blind studies). Three out of four of the RCTs were conducted internationally, with the exception of the PRIME trial, which was exclusively conducted in China. There were some differences in the criteria for assessing response to firstline chemotherapy (complete response/partial response) using CA-125 levels across trials. PRIMA and PRIME included only patients who had CA-125 in the normal range or a >90% decrease in CA-125 during first-line treatment that was stable for at least 7 days and did not increase >15% from the completion of chemotherapy. In contrast, ATHENA-MONO and SOLO-1 enrolled patients who had CA-125 in the normal range Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer

## **HRD Status** 

BRCA and HRD testing was done at screening in PRIMA, PRIME, SOLO-1, and ATHENA-MONO. In PRIME, patients were stratified by germline BRCAm status, whereas other trials did not differentiate between the type (germline vs somatic) of BRCAm. Additionally, PRIME and ATHENA-MONO used a different HRD assay in comparison with the other trials (Table 88).

## **Subsequent Therapies** 

Only PRIMA explicitly reported that cross-over was not permitted; this was not reported for all other studies. Nevertheless, 14% of patients in the placebo arm received subsequent niraparib and 3% of niraparib patients were retreated with niraparib in a subsequent line. The percent of patients receiving subsequent PARPi varied across trials (i.e., PRIMA, SOLO-1, and ATHENA-MONO), subgroups, and treatment arms. These discrepancies would likely bias and diminish the reliability of indirect comparisons for OS and PFS2, as these outcomes directly depend on the effect of subsequent treatments. Additionally, there is no data available on subsequent treatments in PRIME, and thus it is not possible to know how it compares with PRIMA, ATHENA-MONO, and SOLO-1. Due to limited data (e.g., missing information on specific line / intended use of PARPi’s [treatment vs maintenance], and specific PARPi treatments received), it would not be possible to properly adjust for differences in subsequent treatments across trials.

## **Treatment Characteristics** 

All four trials were placebo-controlled. There was consistency in the administration and frequency of the placebo arm. There are some differences in treatment duration across trials, with this being up to 36 months in niraparib trials (PRIMA, PRIME) compared to up to 24 months in ATHENA-MONO and SOLO-1. Additionally, in PRIMA, patients who were deemed to benefit from treatment by the investigator had the option to continue receiving treatment beyond 3 years, but this was not mandatory.

## **Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria** 

General similarities: 

- All RCTs included in the ITC FA enrolled patients with high-grade serous or endometrioid ovarian cancer, including primary peritoneal and fallopian tube cancers, at FIGO stages III/IV. 

- All RCTs required patients to have had a clinical complete or partial response following first-line chemotherapy. 

Notable differences across trials: 

- There was variability in surgical history requirements across trials: the PRIMA trial enrolled Stage III patients with visible residual disease after primary debulking surgery but excluded those with complete cytoreduction, whereas the ATHENA-MONO, SOLO-1 and PRIME trials included patients irrespective of residual disease status 

- In ATHENA-MONO and SOLO-1, complete response was defined as the absence of measurable disease on post-treatment scans or investigator assessed complete response. While in PRIMA complete response was as per RECIST v1.1 

- CA-125 criteria varied across the trials, patients enrolled in PRIMA were required to have either a normal CA-125 level or a >90% reduction in CA-125 following frontline platinum-based treatment 

- In the PRIMA trial, it was required that all residual disease following chemotherapy be 2 cm or less, a criterion not specified in other trials 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 307 -->

- SOLO-1 only recruited patients with BRCA mutations, while the other trials recruited patients regardless of BRCA mutation status. 

- Prior use of bevacizumab was permitted in most trials (PRIMA, PRIME, ATHENA-MONO) and prohibited in the SOLO-1 trial. 

The eligibility criteria for these trials exhibit considerable heterogeneity, underscoring substantial differences in the target populations that these trials aimed to study. The different eligibility criteria for BRCA mutation status, surgical history, and prior bevacizumab use could lead to substantial imbalances in baseline distributions, limiting the comparability of outcomes across the trials. 

## **Clinical Risk Status** 

PRIMA enrolled patients at a high risk of disease progression, whereas the comparator studies enrolled a mix of low and high-risk patients. In particular, only PRIMA excluded Stage III patients with complete cytoreduction (no visible residual disease [VRD]) following primary debulking surgery (PDS)—who would have a lower risk of progression. As clinical risk is a key treatment effect modifier, it is necessary to restrict any ITCs based on PRIMA to the high-risk population for valid statistical inference. SOLO-1 reported outcomes in a comparable 'PRIMA-like' population (i.e., high-risk subgroups, Table 91). 

It must be noted that outcomes in a comparable 'PRIMA-like' high-risk population were not reported in the ATHENA-MONO and PRIME studies.

## **Baseline Characteristics** 

Available baseline characteristics in the intent-to-treat (ITT) population and high-risk subgroups of interest for ITCs are summarised in this section. 

## Overall Population 

For comparisons vs rucaparib (ATHENA-MONO), subgroup analyses for ATHENAMONO have not been published in a PRIMA-like population (i.e., excluding the lowerrisk stage III patients without VRD). Therefore, it was only possible to compare niraparib (based on data from PRIME rather than PRIMA) with rucaparib (ATHENAMONO) in a broader population comprising a mix of both low and high-risk patients. 

Patient-level data were not available for either rucaparib (ATHENA-MONO) or niraparib (PRIME), making only unadjusted ITCs (e.g., Bucher’s method) possible. Baseline characteristics were compared to identify noteworthy imbalances in EMs that could distort a Bucher ITC. Substantial differences were found in the distributions of age, ECOG performance scores and responses to 1L chemotherapy across the trials, which may bias an ITC of ATHENA-MONO versus PRIME. Additionally, there were imbalances in CA-125 levels, primary tumour locations, histology, and proportion of patients with BRCA mutations (Table 92).

## - BRCAm and High Risk Subgroup 

The ITC of interest for the BRCAm and high-risk subgroup is between olaparib (SOLO1) vs niraparib (PRIMA). ## **Outcome Definitions** 

Outcome definitions for overall survival (OS) were consistently defined and comparable across all studies. However, noteworthy differences in PFS definition and assessment schedules were identified across trials. In particular, PFS (investigatorassessed and IRC-assessed) SOLO-1 consider progression an event, regardless of whether a patient received another anti-cancer therapy prior to progression; in contrast, PRIMA, PRIME, and ATHENA-MONO censored PFS at the last evaluable assessment prior to initiation of subsequent anti-cancer therapy. In PRIMA, only 15 out of 733 patients (2%) were censored at their last assessment before follow-up therapy. Therefore, this difference in censoring rules across studies is expected to have a minimal impact on ITC results. PFS definitions in PRIME and ATHENA-MONO are aligned, making Bucher ITCs of PFS from these studies possible.

## **Assessment Schedule for Tumour Response** 

Progression is evaluated at tumour assessment visits scheduled over the course of follow-up in each study, compared in the table below; differences in assessment schedules may introduce bias in ITCs -- known as assessment time bias. Consistent with the tumour assessment schedule in PRIMA, tumour response was assessed every 12 weeks in PRIME, ATHENA-MONO (up to 3 years), and SOLO-1 (up to 3 years). After the first 3 years, the assessment schedules in ATHENA-MONO and SOLO-1 changed from every 12 weeks to every 24 weeks.

## _**comparisons**_ 

Due to a lack of head-to-head studies, ITC methods were required to estimate the relative efficacy and safety of niraparib vs relevant comparators of interest. Bucher's method for ITCs was applied where suitable, specifically in cases where trials were Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 314 -->

linked through a common anchor arm, and it was clinically reasonable to assume that the distributions of treatment effect modifiers were balanced across trials. Simulated treatment comparisons (STCs) were considered within the BRCAm population but were deemed inappropriate an unreliable due to counter-intuitive associations between PFS and both ECOG and age. 

## **STC** 

An STC was explored by fitting parametric survival regression models using patientlevel data from PRIMA (i.e., the index trial) to indirectly compare PFS across studies. **In the anchored setting** , let us consider an index trial, AB, which investigates the relative efficacy of treatment B versus treatment A. We wish to make a comparison versus trial AC, which investigates the relative efficacy of treatment C versus treatment A. In this context, the common treatment, A, serves as an _**anchor**_ , linking the studies and forming a network. In its general form, the STC regression model is given as: 

𝑔(𝜃𝑖) = 𝛽0 + 𝛽𝑇𝑇𝑖 + 𝜷𝑋𝑿𝒊 + 𝜷𝑍𝒁𝒊 + 𝜷𝑇𝑍(𝑇𝑖𝒁𝑖) where g( ⋅ ) is a suitable link function, 𝜃𝑖 is the expected outcome for the i-th patient with treatment 𝑇𝑖 in trial AB, 𝛽0 is the intercept, 𝛽𝑇 is the coefficient for active treatment, 𝜷𝑋 is the vector of coefficients for prognostic variables denoted by 𝑿 , 𝜷𝑍 denotes the vector of coefficients for EMs 𝒁 , and 𝜷𝑇𝑍 is the vector of coefficients for interactions between treatment and EMs. 

STC can be used to estimate either marginal or conditional treatment effects. The conventional implementation of STC (i.e., by centering the covariates to mean values in the comparator population as described in the previous section) targets a conditional estimand. In the case of non-collapsible measures of effect (e.g., hazard ratios), marginal and conditional estimands do not coincide due to nonlinearity. This can cause systematic bias in STC if we were to compare an adjusted conditional HR 𝑑𝐵𝐴(𝐴𝐶) with the marginal HRs 𝑑𝐶𝐴(𝐴𝐶) reported for the comparators. 

𝑑[̂] 𝐵𝐶(𝐴𝐶) = 𝑑𝐵𝐴(𝐴𝐶) − 𝑑𝐶𝐴(𝐴𝐶) 

Therefore, we used an extension of conventional STC all analyses, which enables the estimation of marginal effects. The specific steps followed in the STC analyses to estimate marginal HRs are summarized in the following table.

## **Bucher ITC** 

A Bucher ITC involves a similar anchored comparison of 𝑑𝐵𝐴 and 𝑑𝐶𝐴 as STC, but instead of comparing the adjusted marginal effect of B versus A (i.e., 𝑑𝐵𝐴(𝐴𝐶) ) versus the unadjusted relative effect of C versus A (i.e., 𝑑𝐶𝐴 ), as in anchored STC, the unadjusted marginal effect of B versus A (i.e., 𝑑𝐵𝐴 ) is contrasted with the unadjusted marginal effect of C versus A (i.e., 𝑑𝐶𝐴 ). As PFS is the only outcome to be compared using Bucher ITC, 𝑑 generally represents log HRs on PFS. 

That is, a Bucher ITC between B and C is estimated using the published marginal effect for B versus A and the published marginal effect for C versus A:

## **trials** 

Participant flow in the PRIMA and PRIME trials is provided below. 

## **B.1.2.1 PRIMA** 

Nine hundred eighty nine patients were screened[12] and 733 patients were enrolled in the PRIMA trial, with 487 randomised to the niraparib group and 246 to the placebo Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 320 -->

group (ITT population).[16] Three patients in the niraparib group and two in the placebo group did not receive the assigned treatment.[16] 

As of the data cutoff on April 8, 2024, 27 patients were still receiving niraparib and 11 were still on placebo, while 457 and 233 patients, respectively, had discontinued treatment.[16] Twenty-nine patients in the niraparib group and 7 in the placebo group completed 36 months of treatment.[16] Consent withdrawal occurred in 14 patients in the niraparib group and 3 patients in the placebo group.[16] Details on participant flow in the ITT population and the HRd subgroup are shown in Figure 31.

## **B.1.2.2 PRIME** 

Of 510 screened patients, 384 were randomised in the PRIME trial, with 255 assigned to niraparib and 129 to the placebo group.[13] At the data cut-off (September 30, 2021), 102 niraparib patients and 29 placebo patients were still undergoing treatment.[13] Consent withdrawal occurred in 27 patients treated with niraparib and 5 patients from the placebo group (Figure 32).[13] Details on participant flow in the ITT population are shown in Figure 32.

## **B1.3 Critical appraisal for each study** 

Risk of bias was assessed in six RCTs.[20] All six RCTs were assessed as being at low risk of bias overall; all were double-blind, provided details of the randomisation process, and had baseline characteristics that were evenly balanced between treatment arms (Table 99).[20] 

The single-arm trial, OVARIO,[137] was found to be at moderate risk of bias due to 

concerns around the awareness of the investigators of the intervention received by Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 322 -->

study participants and concerns with handling of missing data.[20] The single-arm trial by Oda 2024[138] was not assessed, since there was no full-text publication available (and insufficient information in the congress abstract).[20] 

Twenty-one RWE studies were assessed for risk of bias.[20] Across the RWE studies, the overall risk of bias was deemed moderate (Table 100).[20] This was due to the potential for confounding, which is greater in observational studies.[20] The only study deemed at low risk of bias was PRED1CT.[20,92]

## **C1.4 Impact of niraparib dosing on efficacy** 

## **C.1.4.1 PRIMA** 

xxxxxx 44 shows the changes in niraparib dosing during the PRIMA trial. Between 13% to 55% of patients who initially received 300 mg (individual or fixed dosing) were on a 100 mg dose after 12 months, and 33% to 81% were on a 200 mg dose. For patients who started treatment at 200 mg, the dose was reduced to 100 mg in 58% of cases.

## **Appendix E: Published cost-effectiveness studies** 

## **E1.1 Identification and selection of relevant studies** 

A non-clinical SLR was undertaken to identify published economic evaluations and cost-effectiveness studies of treatments for people with advanced epithelial (FIGO stage III to IV) high-grade ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer in the 1L maintenance setting.[153] Studies were identified using a search strategy across relevant platforms (via the Ovid platform, as well as conference proceedings and HTA websites).[153] Inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied to studies to determine those most relevant for this submission.[153] This appendix details the objectives, methodology and findings of the SLR. 

The SLR was originally conducted in February 2019 and was subsequently updated in February 2020, March 2023 and February 2025.[153] 

## **E.1.1.1 Search strategy** 

The 2019 SLR and subsequent updates were conducted based on the reporting standards of the PRISMA, general methodological requirements outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions[103] and key HTA bodies, such as NICE.[153] 

The literature database searches included a combination of free-text and controlled vocabulary terms specific to each database.[153] Systematic literature searches were conducted via the Ovid platform to identify peer-reviewed studies of interest in the following electronic literature databases:[153] 

- MEDLINE and MEDLINE In-process 

- Embase 

- Evidence-Based Medicine Reviews: CENTRAL 

- NHS EED (via CRD) 

- National Health Service HTA (via INAHTA for 2025 update) 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved Page 379 of 559 



<!-- page 382 -->

- INAHTA 

- Sheffield Centre for Health and Related Research Health Utilities Database 

- EuroQol 

- EconLit (added for 2025 update and not restricted by time to ensure records are identified for the timeframe of the original SLR and previous updates) 

Grey literature searches were also conducted to identify relevant research that may not have been published in peer-reviewed journals.[153] Conferences not indexed in Embase from the previous three years (2023 through February 2025) were handsearched from the respective conference websites.[153] Conference proceedings from the following key conferences were searched:[153] 

- ESGO 

- ASCO 

- ESMO: annual meeting, Asia congress, gynaecological cancers congress and Anticancer Therapies 

- ASGO 

- SGO

## **E.1.1.2 Study selection** 

Once the searches were conducted, the resulting titles and abstracts were uploaded to Distiller Systematic Review software.[153] The study selection process involved evaluating publications retrieved by the searches against predetermined PICOS criteria to establish the studies that were eligible for inclusion in the SLR.[153] The PICOS criteria used for economic evaluations in the 2025 SLR update are presented in Table 123.[153]

In the first phase of screening, the title and abstract of all records were examined by two independent reviewers to determine their eligibility for inclusion in the SLR.[153] Disagreements between the reviewers were resolved by a third independent reviewer, as necessary.[153] Studies were designated as excluded or included for full-text review based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria described above (Table 123).[153] For abstracts that were deemed relevant during title and abstract screening, the corresponding full-text articles were retrieved for further screening.[153] 

In the second phase of screening, each full-text paper was assessed by two independent reviewers.[153] Disagreements between the reviewers were resolved by a third independent reviewer, as necessary.[153] Studies were designated as excluded or included for full-text review based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria above (Table 123).[153] For each excluded study, a reason for exclusion was specified.[153] 

## **E.1.1.3 Data extraction and quality assessment** 

From the final list of included studies, data were extracted into individual data extraction tables (DET) designed in Microsoft Excel[®] .[153] Data were extracted into the DET by one reviewer, and a second reviewer assessed the entries to ensure consistency and accuracy against the source article as a validation step.[153] 

Quality assessment of the included economic evaluations was conducted using the Drummond checklist.[154] Evidence from conference abstracts was not quality assessed, given the limited information provided.[153] 

## **E.1.1.4 Results** _**Overview of search results**_ 

The original SLR was conducted in February 2019, and an initial update was performed in February 2020, which resulted in the inclusion of 10 publications representing nine unique studies and 2 HTA submissions.[153] A second update was conducted in March 2023, resulting in the inclusion of 42 new publications covering 33 unique studies.[153] In combination with the prior reviews, this resulted in a total of 52 publications, which included 42 unique studies and 17 HTA submissions.[153]

The database searches for the current update were performed on 07 February  2025 and yielded 4,186 records.[153] Of 3,534 unique records screened at the title and abstract level that remained after removing 652 duplicates, 63 were deemed eligible for full-text screening, while the others were excluded.[153] After the full-text review, a total of 10 records were included for synthesis from the database searches, and 5 records were added from grey literature searches (HTA websites).[153] Therefore, a total of 15 records were included in the 2025 SLR update.[153] 

Accounting for the original SLR and subsequent updates, a total of 65 records were included, representing 51 unique studies and included 21 HTA submissions.[153] The PRISMA flow diagram is shown in Figure 46.[153]

## **Appendix F: Health-related quality-of-life studies** 

## **F1.1 Identification and selection of relevant studies** 

Studies reporting on HRQoL outcomes were identified in the clinical SLR (Appendix B1.1), with one additional study reporting on caregiver QoL (Shukla 2022[122] ) identified in the non-clinical SLR (Appendix E1.1 and Appendix G1.1). 

The clinical SLR was conducted in March 2024, with an update in February 2025, to identify evidence on the efficacy, safety and HRQoL of niraparib and relevant comparators in adults with advanced epithelial (FIGO stages III and IV) high-grade ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer who have not progressed following first-line therapy, based on data from clinical trials and real-world evidence studies.[20] 

The non-clinical SLR was conducted in February 2019, with subsequent updates in February 2020, March 2023 and February 2025, to identify utilities and disutilities associated with relevant comparators in patients with advanced epithelial (FIGO stage III to IV) high-grade fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer in the 1L maintenance setting.[153] 

Studies were identified using a search strategy applied across relevant platforms (via the Ovid platform as well as conference proceedings and HTA websites).[20,153] Inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied to studies to determine those most relevant for inclusion in this submission.[20,153] 

## **F.1.1.1 Search strategy** 

The search strategies for the clinical SLR and non-clinical SLR are described in Appendix B.1.1.1 and Appendix E.1.1.1, respectively. 

## **F.1.1.2 Study selection** 

The study selection methodology for the clinical SLR is described in Appendix B.1.1.1.

## **G1.1 Identification and selection of relevant studies** 

A non-clinical SLR was undertaken to identify studies reporting costs and healthcare resource use in people with advanced epithelial (FIGO stages III and IV) high-grade ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer in the 1L maintenance setting.[153] Studies were identified using a search strategy across relevant platforms (via the Ovid platform as well as conference proceedings and HTA websites).[153] Inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied to studies to determine those most relevant for this submission.[153] This appendix details the objectives, methodology and findings of the SLR.[153]

## _**Overview of search results**_ 

Study selection results are described in Appendix E.1.1.4. 

## _**Overview of included studies**_ 

From the original SLR and subsequent updates, a total of 65 records were included following full-text screening. Of these, 15 records, representing 13 unique studies reported on costs/HCRU, including three NICE technology appraisals (Table 132).[153]

## **Appendix J: Clinical Inputs: Survival Analysis** 

## Approach to Curve Selection Process: 

Parametric survival analysis assumes that time to the event of interest follows a parametric distribution. Among the models fitted for each outcome, the most plausible parametric models for the base case and for scenario analysis were chosen for niraparib in line with NICE DSU TSD14 guidance[99] , outlined in Figure 47. The analytical process involves evaluating the fit of each distribution over the observed data period and assessing the face validity beyond the observed period. 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved Page 461 of 559 



<!-- page 464 -->

## **Figure 47. NICE DSU TSD14 guidance for parametric survival model selection** 

**==> picture [387 x 397] intentionally omitted <==**

Abbreviations: AFT = accelerated failure time; AIC = Akaike information criterion; BIC = Bayesian information criterion; PH = proportional hazard 

The analytical process involves evaluating the fit of each distribution over the observed data period and assessing the face validity beyond the observed period. For each population and survival outcome, parametric survival model selection was based on the following four broad categories: 

- Statistical fit: 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved Page 462 of 559 



<!-- page 465 -->

- Statistical fit was assessed using Akaike information criterion (AIC) and Bayesian information criterion (BIC), with the lowest AIC and BIC indicating the model with the best statistical fit to the observed data. 

- While prior application of AIC and BIC rules of thumb in NICE oncology TA appears inconsistent,[202] it can be useful in classifying relative statistical fit for remaining models compared to the distribution with the lowest AIC or BIC. Statistical fit was categorized using modified Burnham/Anderson[203,204] (for AIC) and Kass/Raftery[205] (for BIC) rules of thumb to check the appropriateness of the remaining distributions relative to the best fitting one, with statistical fit classifications from the original papers adapted to ensure completeness, as well as consistency in categorization and interpretation, across rule of thumb categories between measures. The modified rules of thumb for assessing statistical goodness-of-fit are summarized in the table below. 

**Table 144. AIC-BIC rules of thumb** 

|**Rule of thumb category**|**Difference from fit with**<br>**lowest AIC**|**Difference from fit with**<br>**lowest BIC**|
|---|---|---|
|Reasonable|0-7 points|0-7 points|
|Inferior|7-10 points|7-10 points|
|Poor|>10 points|>10 points|



Abbreviations: AIC = Akaike information criterion; BIC = Bayesian information criterion 

- Visual fit: 

   - Visual inspection of the fitted parametric models was performed in relation to the observed K-M curves. 

   - Particular attention may be given to visual fit at the tail, where larger differences between parametric fits are anticipated, but where sudden drops or long plateaus in the K-M curves may be present and associated with low numbers of patients at risk, and therefore must be interpreted with caution. 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved Page 463 of 559 



<!-- page 466 -->

- Hazard profiles: 

   - Smoothed hazard and average hazard rate over time plots for the observed K-M data were compared to hazard plots for each of the parametric distributions to assess which parametric curves provide broad hazard profiles most similar to that implied by the observed data. 

- Clinical plausibility/face validity: 

   - Internal validity 

      - Combinations of chosen parametric survival models were reviewed across outcomes (PFS, OS, TTDD) for each comparator, to ensure plausible combinations of parametric fits are applied (e.g., avoiding implausible overlapping of curves). 

      - Consideration was also given to consistency between population subgroups where relevant. For example, choice of OS extrapolations was reviewed to avoid prediction of higher long-term survival for the BRCAwt subgroup, who are expected to have worse survival prognosis compared to BRCAm patients. 

## `o` External validity 

- Comparing fitted models with long-term data from other RCTs or identified RWE or relevant clinical expert feedback from prior HTA appraisals, where relevant. However, given the focus on the PRIMA trial on high-risk patients and focus on niraparib, a lack of external study data or prior clinical expert feedback was available to help inform long-term niraparib extrapolations. 

- Elicitation of UK clinical expert opinion to assess plausibility (e.g., expectations of the proportion of patients without an event at 10, 15 or 20 years). 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved Page 464 of 559 



<!-- page 467 -->

- General plausibility of combined PFS and OS extrapolations, with PFS and OS anticipated to cross within the modelled time horizon given the lack of expected cure in patients not receiving PARPi maintenance therapy in subsequent treatment lines. 

As assessments of statistical fit, visual fit and hazard profiles only relate to the observed period of available follow-up for the K-M curves, weight given to these criteria in determining the most appropriate model was considered lower than the clinical plausibility of long-term survival extrapolations based on UK clinical expert feedback, given the observed PFS and OS data are not complete and extrapolation beyond the duration of observed data was required.

Abbreviations: PFS = progression-free survival 

To validate the plausibility of long-term survival predictions, PFS BRCAm extrapolations for niraparib were discussed during one-to-one interviews with four UK clinical experts: 

- The first clinical expert indicated an expectation of approximately 24% PFS at 15 years 

- The second clinical expert indicated an expectation of a 10% drop in PFS between 5 to 10 years and expected PFS to be between estimates produced by the log-normal and generalised gamma models at 10 and 20 years (i.e. xxxxx% at 10 years and xxxxx% at 20 years) 

- The third clinical expert indicated survival expectations similar to those produced by the generalised gamma model based on 10 and 20 year predictions (xx% and xx%, respectively) 

- The fourth clinical expert noted an expectation of an additional 5% drop in PFS between 5 and 10 years, resulting in ~xx% PFS at 10 years. The clinical expert therefore stated a preferred for the generalised gamma and spline models as they better reflected the expected drop in PFS between 5 and 10 years, followed by smaller declines between 10 and 15 years. 

For the base case analysis, the generalised gamma model was selected to model niraparib PFS for the BRCAm population. This model provided the best statistical fit among models aligning most closely with the overall range of UK clinical expert feedback at 10 (xxxx%), 15 (xxxx%), and 20 (xxxx%) years, whilst also producing a good visual fit and an appropriate hazard profile compared to that implied by the observed data (increasing then decreasing).

Despite being a poor statistical (13.4 AIC difference and 10.3 BIC difference vs. the lowest) and fairly poor visual fit to the observed KM curve, the log-normal model was explored in a scenario analysis as a more conservative projection given it was suggested by one of the clinical experts as a plausible lower bound for 10-year (xxxx%) and 20-year (xxxx%) PFS for niraparib. A second scenario analysis was also conducted using the 1-knot normal spline, which had the best statistical fit with the lowest AIC and BIC estimates, and provided a slightly more optimistic projection (xxxx%, xxxx%, and xxxx% at 10, 15, and 20 years, respectively) compared to the generalised gamma model (xxxx%, xxxx%, and xxxx% at 10, 15, and 20 years, respectively) while still providing a good visual and hazard profile fit to the observed data.

AIC and BIC classifications of relative fit are outlined in Table 150, including both standard and flexible spline parametric models. The 1-knot normal spline model and the standard parametric generalised gamma produced the best statistical fit according to AIC, with the log-normal model associated with the lowest BIC. - The second expert suggested survival would be somewhere between lognormal and generalised gamma at 10 years (~xx%-xx%) and 20 years (~xx%xx%), with a preference towards the log-normal model due to the PFS/OS crossing point at ~11 years, and suggesting OS may be closer to xx% at 10 years and xx% at 20 years. 

- Although estimates presented for each parametric model were capped by adjusted general population mortality, the third clinical expert struggled to recommend a parametric model suggesting that 30-year OS predictions may be too optimistic in general due to the underlying age of the patient population. 

- The fourth expert noted an expectation of 35-40% OS at 10 years, suggesting that OS of around 36% at 10 years and around 20% at 20 years would be reasonable, and stating a preference for spline models due to the PFS crossing point 

Although the second clinical expert suggested a range between log-normal and generalised gamma, only 1-knot hazard, 2-knot hazard and 1-knot normal spline models provided values within this range and were generally closer to the generalised gamma model, with a drop off in survival predictions for all other standard models compared to generalised gamma and spline models at 10, 15 and 20 years. For the base case analysis, the 1-knot normal model was selected as this model produced the 

joint best overall statistical fit alongside the generalised gamma model, a slightly better visual and statistical fit compared to the log-normal model, and provided the best overall reflection of feedback across clinical experts. Log-normal and generalised gamma were then explored in scenario analyses as potential lower and upper bound OS scenarios for niraparib.

Although the PRIMA trial showed patients continuing on niraparib beyond the maximum treatment duration of 36 months specified within the label, when discussing expectations of time on treatment for niraparib with a UK clinical expert during a oneto-one interview as well as during an advisory board with three UK clinical experts, all of the clinical experts indicated that they expected only a small proportion of patients to continue on niraparib after 36 months in UK clinical practice. Clinicians highlighted that only patients with visible disease would continue on niraparib beyond 36 months, which was rare among patients remaining progression-free who were responding to treatment. Although there was limited evidence to make a strong judgement on whether continued use of niraparib beyond 36 months would have additional benefit, 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer © GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved Page 498 of 559 



<!-- page 501 -->

clinical experts indicated that results of the PRIMA trial suggest that the benefit of the third year of treatment is much less than the first two years, and as such they would be unlikely to prescribe it beyond 36 months. 

During the one-to-one interview, one of the UK clinical experts also stated that they expected no one to remain on niraparib in UK clinical practice at the time of the end of observed follow-up in the PRIMA trial (~78 months). 

Due to the expectation of discontinuation of niraparib by at least 78 months, and the lack of need to extrapolate beyond the observed data, statistical fit and visual fit of the parametric models for niraparib TTDD[99] was used as the primary selection criteria, in line with NICE DSU TSD14 guidance on selection criteria in the presence of complete survival data. However, given that none of the models produced particularly strong visual fits to the data, TTDD was modeled in the base case analysis using the available KM data up to 78 months following by exponential model for any extrapolation required beyond 78 months as the best statistical fit (given the relatively limited differences in visual fit between models with better statistical fits). 

As part of the scenario analyses outlined in Section 3.4.7, niraparib and olaparib TTDD data from SACT were considered for scenario analyses, with available summary-level KM data digitized and pseudo-IPD produced using the Guyot algorithm, and fitted using standard parametric models. Based on AIC/BIC (Table 153), the log-normal model and Gompertz models provided the best statistical fits to the niraparib and Olaparib SACT TTDD KM curves, respectively.

To validate the plausibility of long-term survival extrapolations, niraparib PFS BRCAwt extrapolations from PRIMA were discussed with UK clinical experts. As the first clinical expert provided feedback on PFS expectations for subpopulations within BRCAwt, feedback from the one-to-one interviews conducted with the remaining three clinical experts (those included in the advisory board) for the overall BRCAwt population was utilised to validate PFS expectations: 

- The second clinical expert indicated that estimates between log-normal and generalised gamma models were plausible (approximately xxx% at 10 years)

<!-- page 518 -->

- The fourth clinical expert stated that estimates produced by the spline models and generalised gamma models provided the closest fits to their long-term PFS expectations, suggesting x% or x% PFS at 10 years to be reasonable 

The generalised gamma model, which estimated xxx% PFS at 10 years, was chosen as the base case since it overlapped with the ranges of estimates from all three clinical experts, whilst also providing the best statistical fit along with a good visual and hazard profile fit to the observed data. 

Scenario analysis was conducted using the 2-knot normal spline joint fit model, which provided the best statistical fit among models closer to the upper bound implied by two of the clinical experts (i.e. between xxxx% PFS at 10 years). Although one of the clinical experts suggested <8.0% PFS at 10 years for niraparib may be plausible, all models predicting less than x% PFS at 10 years were substantially lower than 8% (xxx% or lower) and had very poor statistical and visual fits to the observed data (>40 AIC/BIC point differences compared to generalised gamma), and therefore were not considered for scenario analysis.

OS expectations for BRCAwt patients on niraparib were also sought from UK clinical experts. As for PFS, feedback from one-to-one interviews with the latter three clinical experts (those also included in the advisory board) was utilitised due to provision of OS expectations for subgroups within BRCAwt from the first UK clinical expert: 

Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 532 -->

- The second clinical expert stated OS expectations of ~xx% at 10 years and ~5% at 20 years, although noted a preference for log-normal and log-logistic models based on the PFS crossing point 

- The third clinical expert indicated that xx% OS at 10 years was clinically plausible 

- The fourth clinical expert also noted an expectation of approximately xx% OS at 10 years. In addition, the clinical expert stated that they expected PFS and OS to cross between 15 and 20 years, suggesting that estimates produced by the 3-knot spline hazards model were most appropriate 

For the base case analysis, the 1-knot hazard spline model was selected as it represented a reasonable balance of OS expectations between clinical experts, and producing the closest value to xx% at 10 years stated by the first clinical expert. It also provided a fairly good overall relative statistical fit (1 AIC point difference from the lowest, 4.7 BIC point difference from the lowest) and a slightly better visual fit to the observed data compared to the log-normal distribution (which appeared to slightly underpredict the tail of the observed data), in addition to producing an appropriate hazard profile in relation to that implied by the observed data. Similar to the BRCAm population, scenario analyses were then conducted using models that provided the best statistical fits among models representative of the approximate lower and upper bound expectations across the clinical expert feedback collected (log-normal and generalised gamma, respectively).

Although the PRIMA trial showed that some patients continued on NIRA beyond the maximum treatment duration of 36 months specified within the label, UK clinical experts indicated that they expected only a small proportion of patients to continue on NIRA after 36 months in UK clinical practice. Therefore, as for the BRCAm population, 90% of patients were assumed to discontinue niraparib after 36 months, with the remainder continuing on the selected TTDD extrapolation. Further details on this topic are discussed in Section 3.4.7. 

Due to the expectation of discontinuation of NIRA by at least 83 months, and the lack of need to extrapolate beyond the observed data, statistical fit and visual fit of the parametric models for NIRA TTDD was used as the primary selection criteria, in line with NICE DSU TSD14 guidance[99] on selection criteria in the presence of complete Company evidence submission for niraparib for first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer 

© GlaxoSmithKline UK Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 537 -->

survival data. However, given that none of the models produced particularly strong visual fits to the data (with all models slightly underpredicting parts of the middle of the KM curve), TTDD was modeled using the available KM data combined with the best statistically fitting parametric model (exponential) where required for scenarios requiring extrapolation beyond the available 83 months of follow-up data from PRIMA. 

As part of scenario analyses and similar to the BRCAm population, niraparib TTDD for BRCAwt patients was also modeled using the available KM data from SACT. Based on the AIC/BIC estimates (Table 166), the generalised gamma model provided the best statistical fit to the data.

## **Summary of Information for Patients (SIP):** 

## **The pharmaceutical company perspective** 

## **What is the SIP?** 

The Summary of Information for Patients (SIP) is written by the company who is seeking approval from NICE for their treatment to be sold to the National Health Service (NHS) for use in England. It’s a plain English summary of their submission written for patients participating in the evaluation. It’s not independently checked, although members of the public involvement team at NICE will have read it to double-check for marketing and promotional content before it’s sent to you. 

The Summary of Information for Patients template has been adapted for use at NICE from the Health Technology Assessment International – Patient & Citizens Involvement Group (HTAi PCIG). Information about the development is available in an open-access IJTAHC journal article.

**Generic (brand) name:** niraparib (Zejula)

Niraparib will be used by adults with advanced (stages III and IV according to the Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics), high-grade (fast-growing and aggressive) ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer who have responded well (completely or partially) after completing first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. 

For simplicity, this group will be referred to as "advanced ovarian cancer" in the following sections.

## **Section 2: current landscape** 

## **2a) The condition – clinical presentation and impact** 

Please provide a few sentences to describe the condition that is being assessed by NICE and the number of people who are currently living with this condition in England. 

Please outline in general terms how the condition affects the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers. Please highlight any mortality/morbidity data relating to the condition if available. If the company is making a case for the impact of the treatment on carers this should be clearly stated and explained. 

## **Ovarian cancer overview and its causes:** 

Ovarian cancer is a term used to describe different types of cancer[1] that affect female reproductive organs, including the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and the peritoneum.[2] It is classified into four stages (I–IV) defined by the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), which describe how far the cancer has spread.[3] Stages III and IV are considered advanced disease because the cancer has spread beyond the pelvis to other parts of the body.[4] Ovarian cancer is the sixth most common cancer among women in the United Kingdom.[5,6] In 2022, there were 7,078 new cases of ovarian cancer, with approximately 60% of these being advanced cases.[5] Additionally, 19,325 patients were living with ovarian cancer, having been diagnosed within the last five years.[6] 



<!-- page 564 -->

**==> picture [437 x 215] intentionally omitted <==**

The exact causes of ovarian cancer are unknown, however it is estimated that approximately 50% of ovarian cancer cases are the result of abnormalities in how normal cells function.[7] These abnormal cells are referred to as ‘homologous repair deficient’, or HRd for short, as they lack certain functions that help them stay healthy.[7] Patients who do not have HRd are referred to as homologous repair proficient, or HRp for short. The most common reason for a cell being HRd is due to an abnormal BRCA gene, commonly referred to as a BRCA mutation.[38] It is estimated that people with harmful BRCA mutations have a 16% to 65% higher risk of getting ovarian cancer, especially the fast-growing type.[1,9] 

**==> picture [421 x 220] intentionally omitted <==**

**Impact of ovarian cancer on patients and their families:** Before the spread of disease, the symptoms of ovarian cancer are usually vague and can resemble those of less serious conditions, which can delay diagnosis.[10-12] The most common symptoms include abdominal or pelvic pain, increased abdominal size or bloating, and changes in bowel habits.[13] 

In advanced stages, ovarian cancer significantly affects patients' lives beyond just their physical health.[14] It impacts their emotional, social, and psychological wellbeing.[14] A survey of UK ovarian cancer patients found that many patients with 



<!-- page 565 -->

advanced disease experience fear and uncertainty, leading to anxiety and depression.[14] 

## **Mortality and morbidity of ovarian cancer** 

Ovarian cancer is a serious and life-threatening disease. In 2022, it caused 4,159 deaths in the United Kingdom, making it the fifth most common cause of cancerrelated deaths among women.[6] How long a patient may live with ovarian cancer depends on many factors, including the stage of the disease, genetic mutations, and whether the tumour can be removed entirely by surgery.[15] 

Advanced ovarian cancer is rarely curable with current treatments, which include surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy.[16-19] After initial treatment, about 80% of patients experience cancer recurrence which is typically treated with additional chemotherapy.[3,20] Unfortunately, as the disease comes back treatment with chemotherapy isn’t as effective and the benefits do not last as long. It is not uncommon for some people to experience the cancer reoccurring multiple times and having to receive chemotherapy again. The repeated re-occurrence of cancer and repeated treatment with chemotherapy have a large impact on how patients feel and their overall quality of life. 

Maintenance treatments, such as niraparib, are used after first-line chemotherapy and their intent is to keep ovarian cancer from returning or worsening. By stopping or delaying the disease, women can live longer without symptoms of their cancer returning or the having to deal with the effects of repeated chemotherapy. Evidence shows that the longer a person lives without disease relapse, the lower the likelihood the cancer will return at all. 

## **2b) Diagnosis of the condition (in relation to the medicine being evaluated)** 

Please briefly explain how the condition is currently diagnosed and how this impacts patients. Are there any additional diagnostic tests required with the new treatment? 

## **Ovarian cancer diagnosis** 

Diagnosing ovarian cancer involves following steps and tests:[1] 

- **Physical examination and medical history:** The process begins with a thorough physical examination, and the doctor asks detailed questions about the patient’s medical history and symptoms that suggest ovarian cancer. 

- **Laboratory tests:** Blood tests are conducted to measure specific substances (biomarkers) that can be abnormal in ovarian cancer, including CA-125, CEA, and CA-19-9 (proteins in the blood that help to diagnose and monitor certain cancers). 

- **Imaging testing:** Ultrasound and computed tomography (CT) scans are used to get detailed images of the ovaries and other areas. Ultrasounds help detect abnormalities in the ovaries, while CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis help determine the extent of the disease (staging) and assist in planning surgery. 



<!-- page 566 -->

- **Pathological examination:** To confirm the diagnosis, a sample of the tumour is needed. Pathologists examine a sample of cells under a microscope to confirm if it is ovarian cancer. 

- **Genetic testing:** For all patients with fast-growing ovarian cancer, it is recommended to test for genetic mutations in the BRCA genes (BRCAm) and for homologous repair deficiency (HRD). These tests can help in understanding the genetic factors involved and in planning appropriate treatments. 

Niraparib treatment does not require any additional diagnostic tests beyond those already performed for diagnosing and staging the cancer.[21]

## **2c) Current treatment options:** 

The purpose of this section is to set the scene on how the condition is currently managed: 

- What is the treatment pathway for this condition and where in this pathway the medicine is likely to be used? Please use diagrams to accompany text where possible. Please give emphasis to the specific setting and condition being considered by NICE in this review. For example, by referencing current treatment guidelines. It may be relevant to show the treatments people may have before and after the treatment under consideration in this SIP. 

- Please also consider: 

   - if there are multiple treatment options, and data suggest that some are more commonly used than others in the setting and condition being considered in this SIP, please report these data. 

   - are there any drug–drug interactions and/or contraindications that commonly cause challenges for patient populations? If so, please explain what these are. 

## **Treatment of newly diagnosed patients:** 

Managing advanced, newly diagnosed ovarian cancer involves a team approach with surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy **.**[1,3,22,23] Treatment is tailored based on patient factors such as age, overall health, and the ability to achieve complete tumour removal, and includes:[1,3] 



<!-- page 567 -->

- **Primary debulking surgery followed by chemotherapy** : This is when patients undergo surgery to completely remove, or remove as much as possible, any visible cancer. Following surgery, patients are then treated with chemotherapy to further damage any cancer cells remaining after the surgery. One course of chemotherapy typically comprises of 6 doses, spaced 3 weeks apart. This is often referred to as ‘6 cycles’ of chemotherapy. 

- **Neoadjuvant (given before surgery) chemotherapy followed by interval debulking surgery and chemotherapy** : For patients who may not be good candidates for immediate surgery, some initial chemotherapy can reduce tumour size before surgery, with the goal of making the tumour suitable for surgical removal. After surgery, additional chemotherapy is given to further damage any cancer cells remaining after the surgery. 

- **Chemotherapy alone:** For patients who cannot undergo surgery due to advanced disease or other health issues. 

The goal of surgical treatment, whether primary or interval, is to remove as much of the tumour as possible. Less disease remaining after surgery is associated with lower risk of relapse and longer life expectancy.[1,3,22,23] 

The standard chemotherapy approach involves the use of a platinum agent (carboplatin or cisplatin) in combination with a taxane (paclitaxel or docetaxel).[1,3,22,23] Additionally, bevacizumab, which targets blood vessel growth in tumours,[1] can be added to chemotherapy with the aim to improve treatment outcomes in some patients.[24] 

**==> picture [440 x 309] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Maintenance treatment after first-line therapy:** 

Maintenance therapy using poly-(ADP)-ribose polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) is now considered the standard care for ovarian cancer.[1,3,22,23] This type of treatment helps prevent the cancer from coming back after initial chemotherapy.[1,3,22,23] 



<!-- page 568 -->

Currently, in England, there are three different PARPis approved as maintenance therapy for advanced ovarian cancer in patients who responded to first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. These drugs are suitable for different patient groups: 

- **Olaparib** : recommended only for patients with BRCA mutations[25] 

- **Rucaparib** : recommended for patients without BRCA mutations who are HRd or are HRp or have unknown HRD status, especially if bevacizumab is not an option for them,[26 ] 

- **Niraparib** : currently available through the Cancer Drugs Fund for maintenance treatment without restrictions related to genetic mutations.[27 ] 

Some patients who received bevacizumab as part of their initial chemotherapy treatment can also continue to use bevacizumab on its own if they are HRp, or in combination with olaparib as a maintenance treatment if they are HRd.[24,28,29 ] 

This application is for the continued availability of niraparib as a maintenance treatment for all patients with advanced ovarian cancer under standard reimbursement policies.

## **2d) Patient-based evidence (PBE) about living with the condition** 

Context: 

- **Patient-based evidence (PBE)** is when patients input into scientific research, specifically to provide experiences of their symptoms, needs, perceptions, quality of life issues or experiences of the medicine they are currently taking. PBE might also include carer burden and outputs from patient preference studies, when conducted in order to show what matters most to patients and carers and where their greatest needs are. Such research can inform the selection of patient-relevant endpoints in clinical trials. 

In this section, please provide a summary of any PBE that has been collected or published to demonstrate what is understood about **patient needs and disease experiences** . Please include the methods used for collecting this evidence. Any 



<!-- page 569 -->

such evidence included in the SIP should be formally referenced wherever possible and references included. 

## **Patient-based evidence:** 

A survey of 142 UK ovarian cancer patients revealed that they face significant emotional, social, and psychological challenges.[14] The study reported that: 

- 58% of patients felt their emotional well-being was severely affected, 

- 66% felt it severely impacted their ability to plan for the future, 

- 49% reported a severe impact on their personal identity, 

- 45% experienced severe impacts on their relationships with a spouse or partner, 

- 40% saw significant effects on their family and social life, 

- 51% reported severe impacts on sleep.[14] 

Additionally, more than 70% of patients experienced moderate to severe anxiety and nervousness, 64% felt frightened or angry, 57% felt helpless, and 56% felt numb or empty.[14] 

Patients' emotional well-being is a major concern after completing first-line treatment for advanced ovarian cancer.[30-32] The uncertainty about their future health, due to the lack of ongoing treatment, causes significant anxiety and fear for up to 80% of women who worry about the high risk of cancer returning.[30-32] As a result, many patients prefer receiving maintenance therapy, which is ongoing treatment to help keep the cancer from returning, rather than active surveillance, which involves regular monitoring without any treatment.[33,34] Maintenance therapy can help limit the psychological impact of disease on patients, with fewer patients who receive maintenance therapy reporting anger and resentment (49% vs 83%), anxiety and nervousness (63% vs 81%), and fear (55% vs 77%) compared with those being actively monitored.[14]

## **Section 3: the treatment** 

## **3a) How does the new treatment work? What are the important features of this treatment?** 

Please outline as clearly as possible important details that you consider relevant to patients relating to the mechanism of action and how the medicine interacts with the body 

Where possible, please describe how you feel the medicine is innovative or novel, and how this might be important to patients and their communities. 

If there are relevant documents which have been produced to support your regulatory submission such as a summary of product characteristics or patient information leaflet, please provide a link to these. 

## **How niraparib works** 

Niraparib is a type of anti-cancer medicine called a PARP inhibitor. PARP inhibitors block an enzyme called poly [adenosine diphosphate-ribose] polymerase (PARP), which helps cells repair damaged DNA. By blocking PARP, niraparib prevents cancer cells from repairing their DNA, leading to cell death and helping to stop the cancer spreading.[21] Studies have shown niraparib is effective in causing damage to cancer cells (which can in turn kill them), regardless of whether they have mutations in the BRCA genes or not, and whether they have HRd or not.[21]

## **3c) Administration and dosing** 

How and where is the treatment given or taken? Please include the dose, how often the treatment should be given/taken, and how long the treatment should be given/taken for. 

How will this administration method or dosing potentially affect patients and caregivers? How does this differ to existing treatments? 

## **Niraparib administration and dosing:** 

The starting dose of niraparib depends on the patient's body weight and platelet count in the blood:[21] 

- For patients weighing <77 kg or with a baseline platelet count <150,000/μL: **200 mg** (two 100-mg tablets) taken orally once daily. 

- For patients weighing ≥77 kg with a baseline platelet count ≥150,000/μL: **300 mg** (three 100-mg tablets) taken orally once daily. 

Patients should take their dose at the same time each day, preferably at bedtime, to help manage nausea. If a dose is missed, patients should take the next dose at the usual scheduled time.[21] 

Treatment should continue until the disease worsens or returns or side effects become unmanageable. Some PARPis are recommended for a maximum of 2 years, reflecting how they were used in the clinical trials. Niraparib is typically used for up to 3 years, provided that patients do not experience serious side effects or worsening of the cancer. 

Side effects can occur as part of treatment but are generally managed with dose adjustments or with interruptions to treatment as necessary; serious side effects may require treatment to be stopped completely.[21] Some side effects are usually experienced during the initial phase of treatment so it recommended to monitor for these by testing blood pressure and blood counts over this time.[21] The general approach to managing side effects involves initially stopping the treatment for up to 28 days to allow recovery, then restarting at the same dose.[21] If the side effects return, treatment should be stopped again and restarted at a lower dose (as shown below).[21] If the side effects continue beyond the 28-day break or cannot be managed with these breaks and dose reductions, niraparib needs to be stopped completely.[21] There are some instances when treatment with niraparib should be discontinued immediately, such as when a person develops blood disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome/acute myeloid leukaemia (MDS/AML).[21 ] 

The administration method and dosing of niraparib are designed to be straightforward and should not have a negative impact on patients or caregivers. 



<!-- page 572 -->

One advantage of niraparib compared to other PARP inhibitors is its packaging. Niraparib comes in a form that allows easy dose adjustments without the need for different packaging with various doses. This flexibility can simplify treatment management and reduce the treatment burden.
