## **3d) Current clinical trials** 

Please provide a list of completed or ongoing clinical trials for the treatment. Please provide a brief top-level summary for each trial, such as title/name, location, population, patient group size, comparators, key inclusion and exclusion criteria and completion dates etc. Please provide references to further information about the trials or publications from the trials. 

## **Clinical trials for niraparib:** 

Two clinical trials, **PRIMA** and **PRIME** , were conducted to study niraparib as a maintenance therapy after first-line maintenance treatment for advanced ovarian cancer. 

**PRIMA** was designed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of niraparib as a maintenance therapy for advanced ovarian cancer.[35] The study was a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial.[35] This means that it took place at multiple hospitals and clinics, patients were randomly assigned to different treatment groups to avoid bias, and neither patients nor doctors knew which treatment each patient was receiving (niraparib or placebo – no active treatment) to avoid this knowledge influencing results.[35] 

The study included adult women with confirmed advanced (stage III or IV) ovarian cancer who had previously undergone a platinum-based chemotherapy and had responded well to it.[35] This trial disproportionately included patients who were at a higher risk of their cancer returning, and excluded some patients who had a lower risk of disease returning (e.g., those who had no signs of disease after surgery).[35] A total of 733 patients participated in the study. They were divided into two groups – one group received niraparib (487 patients) and the other group received a placebo (246 patients), which appeared identical to niraparib capsules.[35] Among 



<!-- page 573 -->

the participants, 246 patients in the niraparib group and 126 patients in the placebo group had HRd.[35 ] 

**PRIME** had very similar methodology to PRIMA and included patients with advanced ovarian cancer, however this trial didn’t limit patients joining the trial based on how likely their cancer was to return.[36] This study was conducted in China, and 255 patients received niraparib, while 129 patients received a placebo.[36]

## **3e) Efficacy** 

Efficacy is the measure of how well a treatment works in treating a specific condition. 

In this section, please summarise all data that demonstrate how effective the treatment is compared with current treatments at treating the condition outlined in section 2a. 

- Are any of the outcomes more important to patients than others and why? 

- Are there any limitations to the data which may affect how to interpret the results? 



<!-- page 574 -->

Please do not include academic or commercial in confidence information but where necessary reference the section of the company submission where this can be found. 

**PRIMA** is the key clinical trial to provide evidence for the treatment effect of niraparib as a maintenance therapy for advanced ovarian cancer.[35] The main objective of the trial was to investigate how well treatment with niraparib could delay the cancer from returning or worsening (i.e., relapse) following treatment with chemotherapy. Results from the PRIMA study show:[35 ] 

- Niraparib treatment reduced the rate of disease progression (relapse) or death by 57% specifically in patients with HRd ovarian cancer and by 38% in the total trial population 

- Secondary objectives of the trial included investigating if niraparib delayed the need for additional anticancer treatment, and whether patients lived longer overall. Consistent with the primary objective, patients treated with niraparib were able to delay their cancer from getting worse and postpone the need for more treatments compared to those who received placebo. However, the study could not show whether taking niraparib helped patients live longer. This might be because the trial couldn't control how patients were treated when the disease returned, and this can affect how long patients live overall. 

- The PRIMA trial also showed that niraparib helped reduce disease progression, irrespective of the BRCA mutation or HRd status.[35 ] 

The **PRIME** study is very similar to the PRIMA study but includes a broader patient population, which included both higher-risk and lower-risk patients.[36] Results from the PRIME study show:[36 ] 

- Niraparib treatment reduced the rate of disease progression (relapse) or death by 55% in the overall population 

- Secondary objectives of the trial included investigating if niraparib delayed the need for anticancer treatment, and whether patients lived longer overall. 

- • Consistent with the primary objective, treatment with niraparib was shown to delay the need for additional anticancer treatments such as additional chemotherapy. 

- The PRIME trial has not yet been running long enough for it to show whether niraparib results in people living longer overall. However, a trend towards benefit with niraparib treatment was observed. 

Safety results from the PRIMA and PRIME studies are presented in the response to question 3g.

Please include any patient preference information (PPI) relating to the drug profile, for instance research to understand willingness to accept the risk of side effects given the added benefit of treatment. Please include all references as required. 

## **Quality of life results:** 

In the PRIMA study, several commonly used questionnaires that measure quality of life were completed by patients, including:[37] 

- EORTC-QLQ-C30: assess overall health and quality of life and specific domains and symptoms, as physical functioning, pain or fatigue, 

- EORTC-QLQ-OV20: specific for ovarian cancer symptoms, including abdominal/gastrointestinal symptoms, attitude towards disease and treatment, and chemotherapy side effects 

- FOSI: measures symptoms and concerns related to ovarian cancer, 

- EQ-5D-5L: measures general health status. 

During the PRIMA study, the quality of life measured by FOSI did not change much over time in either the niraparib or placebo groups, and the results were similar between the two groups.[37] Health-related quality-of-life, as measured by EQ-5D-5L, slightly improved over time in both groups.[37] Similarly, there were no differences between the groups in terms of overall quality of life, physical functioning, pain, abdominal symptoms, attitude towards the disease and treatment, and chemotherapy side effects, as measured by the EORTC-QLQ-C30 and EORTC-QLQ-C28 questionnaires.[37] However, patients taking niraparib reported less fatigue over time compared to those taking a placebo.[37] Overall, data from the PRIMA trial showed that niraparib did not negatively impact patient quality of life. 

In the PRIME study, the quality of life of patients was not assessed.[36]

In the **PRIMA** study, side effects were reported in both groups of patients, as shown in the table below.[35] Some patients in either treatment group stopped taking the treatments because of the side effects they experienced.[35] The most common side effects experienced by patients receiving niraparib were low number of platelets (thrombocytopenia), low number of red blood cells (anaemia) and feeling sick (nausea).[35] The most common side effects in the placebo group were abdominal pain, fatigue and feeling sick (nausea).[35]

## **3i) Value and economic considerations** 

## **Introduction for patients:** 

Health services want to get the most value from their budget and therefore need to decide whether a new treatment provides good value compared with other treatments. To do this they consider the costs of treating patients and how patients’ health will improve, from feeling better and/or living longer, compared with the treatments already in use. The drug manufacturer provides this information, often presented using a health economic model. 

In completing your input to the NICE appraisal process for the medicine, you may wish to reflect on: 

- The extent to which you agree/disagree with the value arguments presented below (e.g., whether you feel these are the relevant health outcomes, 



<!-- page 580 -->

addressing the unmet needs and issues faced by patients; were any improvements that would be important to you missed out, not tested or not proven?) 

- If you feel the benefits or side effects of the medicine, including how and when it is given or taken, would have positive or negative financial implications for patients or their families (e.g., travel costs, time-off work)? 

- How the condition, taking the new treatment compared with current treatments affects your quality of life. 

Health technology assessment includes economic evaluation to ensure that new treatments provide ‘good value for money’ compared to other available treatments. To do so, it evaluates how much it costs to treat each patient and how much the patients’ health will improve. The company (GSK) provided NICE with the information they need to make this assessment in the form of a health economic model. 

## **How the model reflects advanced ovarian cancer:** 

The goal of the economic model is to compare the costs and quality of life associated with niraparib to the costs and quality of life associated with other available treatment options. If niraparib maximises survival and quality of life for the amount of money it costs, niraparib is considered ‘good value for money’. 

To treat ovarian cancer, patients receive different treatments depending on their BRCA mutation. Because of this, the economic model conducted different analyses for patients with different mutations and who received different treatments. 

**==> picture [426 x 125] intentionally omitted <==**

To determine if a treatment is ‘good value for money’ different outcomes relating to survival, quality of life and side effects were taken from trials and inputted in the model. Data of treatment costs were also added. Different analyses were conducted on these outcomes to predict the treatments cost and impact. 



<!-- page 581 -->

**==> picture [427 x 546] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Uncertainty** 

- When data from clinical trials are projected beyond the end of observed data (follow-up period), there is uncertainty in the predicted outcomes. This can be due to unpredictable events, changes in data, or random factors. 

- To address this, various different analyses were conducted to test the impact of changing variables on results. However, the company determined that there are no specific uncertainties beyond those inherent to any evaluation in advanced ovarian cancer.

This population includes patients regardless of BRCA mutation or HRD status, provided they meet the criteria for platinum response. Therefore, the population for niraparib is broader than that for rucaparib under TA1055, which does not include patients with BRCAm. 

Furthermore, the restriction outlined in TA1055 for rucaparib, which limits its use to non-HRD-positive patients who are ineligible for bevacizumab maintenance, aligns with current clinical practice and the treatment pathway for PARPi monotherapies. Therefore, it does not introduce any additional access restrictions for rucaparib in the non-HRD-positive patient population and is reimbursed in the NHS for all BRCA mutation-negative ovarian cancer patients following a response to 1L PBC.[1] 

As outlined in the submission, PARPi monotherapy is considered for patients who did not receive or were unable to tolerate bevacizumab during induction chemotherapy (Figure 1).

**b) If the company is seeking a recommendation from NICE for niraparib use in patients who would currently receive olaparib + bevacizumab and/or bevacizumab maintenance therapy, please conduct analyses and provide results for all relevant outcomes for niraparib versus olaparib + bevacizumab, and niraparib versus bevacizumab in the relevant populations(based on NICE TA946 and the NHS England BEV3 and BEV10 commissioning approval criteria) using data for niraparib from the** _**PRIMA**_ **trial.** 

NICE TA946 recommends olaparib in combination with bevacizumab, within its marketing authorisation, as maintenance treatment for adults with advanced (FIGO stages III and IV) high-grade epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer that is HRD-positive and has completely or partially responded to _first-line platinum-based chemotherapy with bevacizumab_ .[3] 

Similarly, BEV10 commissioning criteria for bevacizumab as maintenance therapy clearly specifies that bevacizumab monotherapy can only be used following completion of first-line induction chemotherapy in combination with bevacizumab.[2] 

Given the distinct treatment pathway for bevacizumab-based maintenance therapies in advanced ovarian cancer (Figure 1), olaparib + bevacizumab and bevacizumab monotherapy are not relevant comparators for niraparib.

**A3. Priority question. In TA1055, analyses were presented in the HRD-positive (homologous recombination deficient [HRd]), and HRD status negative (homologous recombination proficient [HRp]) or HRD unknown subgroups. The EAG appreciates the company's position about the lack of comparability of PRIMA and ATHENA-MONO; however, the EAG requests that the company conduct the following analyses and include its interpretation of the results in light of these concerns.** 

**Please conduct indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) for niraparib versus rucaparib using data for niraparib from the PRIMA trial and ATHENA-MONO for rucaparib, for the following subgroups (irrespective of BRCA mutation status):** 

- **a) Patients who are HRd. (The EAG notes that there is an imbalance between the 2 trials as far as BRCA status is concerned. The EAG therefore recommends that the company rebalances the PRIMA population for this analysis, for example, using Method of Moments. Alternatively the EAG considers that the company could break randomisation in PRIMA and perform a subgroup analysis using the BRCAwild-type/HRd subgroup from both trials. The EAG’s preference would be to avoid breaking randomisation); and** 

- **b) Patients who are HRp or have unknown HRD status. (The EAG notes that there may not be outcomes data available to include the unknown HRD status subgroup from ATHENA-MONO, in which case, please use only the HRp subgroup data from both trials).** 

**Please provide baseline characteristics for patients in the analyses and the results for overall survival (OS), investigator-assessed progression-free survival (PFS), blinded independent central review (BICR) PFS, progressionfree survival to second progression (PFS2) and time to first subsequent** 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 595 -->

## **therapy (TFST), including the sample sizes, hazard ratio (HR), 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) and p-value.** 

As described in the CS, an ITC comparing PRIMA and ATHENA-MONO was not feasible due to the absence of high-risk subgroup data for ATHENA-MONO. The PRIMA trial was designed to include patients with high-risk characteristics, such as a greater proportion of individuals with known prognostic factors for relapse (e.g., stage IV disease and NACT), while specifically excluding patients with stage III disease without VRD following primary debulking surgery—low-risk patients who generally have the best prognosis. In contrast, ATHENA-MONO included these low-risk patients, with a substantially higher proportion of patients having no visible residual disease compared to PRIMA (75% vs. 46%, respectively in the ITT population).[4,5] Given that clinical risk is a key treatment effect modifier, restricting ITCs based on PRIMA to a high-risk population is essential for valid statistical inference.[6,7] 

A naïve comparison of PFS HRs between PRIMA and ATHENA-MONO indicates no clinically meaningful differences, with any observed variations likely attributable to the exclusion of stage III NVRD patients in the PRIMA trial and the shorter duration of follow-up in ATHENA-MONO. Furthermore, it must be noted that both trials were designed with PFS as the primary endpoint, making it the most reliable outcome for any comparisons. Differences in post-progression treatments and potential unblinding after progression may have introduced bias in secondary outcomes such as PFS2 and OS.

The PRIME study included both high and low-risk patient groups, allowing comparisons between niraparib and rucaparib in a mixed population. However, the proportions of low- and high-risk patients in both ATHENA- MONO and PRIME are unknown, and individual patient data are unavailable for either study. Consequently, Bucher ITCs, which are unadjusted for population differences, was the only feasible approach. 

As noted in Section 2.7.1 of the company submission, there are substantial differences in key prognostic factors/effect modifiers (e.g., ECOG, primary tumour location, histology, BRCAm, response to 1L chemotherapy, CA-125) between PRIME and ATHENA-MONO. These differences generally favoured ATHENA-MONO, except for a higher proportion of BRCAm patients in PRIME. Given the number of limitations, ITCs were conducted across all biomarker subgroups (please see Section 2.7.1 of the company submission and response to A4).

## _**Comparators - olaparib**_ 

**A5. Priority question. The EAG notes that a naïve comparison of the hazard ratio (HR) for investigator-assessed PFS in the ITT population and the highrisk subgroup of SOLO-1 suggests they have similar HRs (0.34 and 0.33, respectively). Please conduct Bucher ITCs for niraparib versus olaparib in the BRCAm population using the ITT population from SOLO-1 and the BRCAm subgroup from PRIMA.** 

**Please provide baseline characteristics for patients in the analyses and the results for OS, investigator-assessed PFS, BICR PFS, PFS2 and TFST, including the sample sizes, hazard ratio (HR), 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) and p-value.** 

Given the substantial differences in patient populations, trial designs, baseline characteristics, and endpoints, conducting a Bucher ITC for niraparib versus olaparib using the ITT population from SOLO-1 and the BRCAm subgroup from PRIMA is not methodologically appropriate. 

SOLO-1 primarily included a low-risk population, with a substantially higher proportion of patients having no visible residual disease post-surgery compared to PRIMA (75% vs. XXXX, respectively in the BRCAm population). Additionally, SOLO-1 had a notably high proportion of patients with favourable ECOG scores (77% had ECOG 0) and disease stage (85% were Stage III).[11] 

It is also important to note that the risk of relapse increases cumulatively with the presence of multiple high-risk factors (e.g., residual disease, Stage IV disease).[12] The 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 599 -->

importance of the presence of multiple risk factors is further demonstrated in PAOLA1 which included a lower proportion of patients with favourable disease characteristics compared to SOLO-1 (e.g., 60% had no visible residual disease and 70% had Stage III disease in the ITT population) and reported outcomes separately for high- and lowrisk groups. High-risk BRCAm patients in PAOLA-1 had higher hazard ratios compared to the low-risk patients within the trial, highlighting the impact of cumulative risk factors on treatment outcomes.[7,8] 

A6. Please conduct Bucher ITCs for niraparib versus olaparib in the BRCAm population using the ITT population from SOLO-1 and the BRCAm subgroup from PRIME. 

Please provide baseline characteristics for patients in the analyses and the results for OS, investigator-assessed PFS, BICR PFS, PFS2 and TFST, including the sample sizes, hazard ratio (HR), 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) and p-value. Unfortunately, IPD from PRIME are not available to facilitate a comparison of baseline characteristics or any outcome other than (BICR) PFS in the BRCAm subgroup. A Bucher ITC of (BICR) PFS between niraparib (using data from the BRCAm subgroup from PRIME) and olaparib (using data from the ITT population from SOLO-1) is the only comparison that is feasible based on the available data. The results are shown in the table below. 

However, we would like to emphasise that this comparison may be subject to substantial bias due to potential imbalances in baseline characteristics (which cannot be verified). A further limitation is that the assumption of proportional hazards may not hold both within the BRCAm subgroup of PRIME and the ITT population of SOLO-1 (based on log cumulative hazard plot, Schoenfeld residuals and HR and time interaction, see response to Question B11 and the Appendix). For these reasons, this comparison should be interpreted with caution.

Please provide the results including Kaplan-Meier plots for OS, investigatorassessed PFS, BICR PFS, PFS2, TTD and TFST for the subgroup of patients with BRCA mutation-negative HRD ‑ negative or HRD ‑ unknown advanced ovarian cancer who would not be eligible for treatment with bevacizumab because they do not meet the commissioning approval criteria. 

- a) PRIMA; 

## b) PRIME. 

It is not feasible to conduct these analyses using data from the PRIMA trial, as the relevant patient group (those not meeting the commissioning approval criteria for bevacizumab) was not included in the study. 

According to commissioning criteria BEV3, patients are not eligible for bevacizumab as an add-on to first-line platinum-based chemotherapy if they have stage 3 disease with no visible residual disease following primary debulking surgery. This group of lowrisk patients aligns with those excluded from the PRIMA trial. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 613 -->

Furthermore, as per commissioning criteria BEV10, patients are not eligible for bevacizumab as a maintenance treatment unless they received bevacizumab during induction alongside chemotherapy. In the PRIMA trial, only a negligible number of patients had prior exposure to bevacizumab, and discontinued treatment following enrolment to the study (N=7/733). 

Similarly, the PRIME study does not provide individual patient data, which prevents us from performing subgroup analyses.

## **XXXXXX** 

The hazard ratio of XXX observed in patients with FIGO Stage IV disease should be interpreted with caution. The PRIMA trial was not stratified by stage of disease, and the study was not designed to evaluate treatment effects specifically in this subgroup. Small sample sizes and retrospective nature of the analysis further limit the reliability of these findings, as no formal testing was performed. Additionally, it is challenging to isolate the effects of individual factors. 

While this observation may be explained in part by small imbalances (<10% difference) in some of the baseline characteristics between the Stage IV niraparib and placebo 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 614 -->

arms (examples include: ECOG PS, Region), it is unlikely that a singular or subset of molecular, clinical or demographic characteristics is causative of the trend observed for OS. 

Stage IV disease at diagnosis is independently prognostic of poor long-term outcomes and is also known to be associated with other risk factors for disease progression and death, including use of neoadjuvant chemotherapy and postoperative residual disease.[14-16] In the PRIMA trial, variations were observed in the number and location of new lesions in patients with stage III and IV disease at diagnosis who experienced disease progression. These variations may have contributed to differences in the overall prognoses of these patient subgroups. 

## _**Assumptions of equivalence**_ 

## **A14. Priority question. Within the CS, the company makes multiple references to the equivalence between treatments. Please can the company:** 

## **a) Clarify if formal equivalence testing was performed to reach such conclusions.** 

We would like to clarify that no formal testing of equivalence was previously performed. 

## **b) Perform formal equivalence testing, if not previously performed, to provide evidence to support, or otherwise, the company’s claims of equivalence between treatments.** 

The ideal setting for testing equivalence between niraparib and comparator treatments would have been a non-inferiority trial. No manufacturer has undertaken a head-tohead non-inferiority trial of PARPi monotherapies in ovarian cancer. Therefore, it is not possible to undertake robust formal non-inferiority testing of these treatments. 

To address the above request, we ran post-hoc analyses (described in Kaul and Diamond 2007), referred to as "fixed margin analysis".[17] However, we emphasise that these post-hoc analyses typically suffer from lack of statistical power and can only be interpreted as exploratory. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 615 -->

Fixed margin analyses seek to determine whether the new treatment (i.e. niraparib) is inferior to the standard treatment (e.g. olaparib or rucaparib) by no more than some predefined margin. They are applicable when the comparator study has demonstrated that the standard treatment (e.g. rucaparib or olaparib) is superior to placebo. According to the “mixed margin analysis”, the maximum noninferiority margin, 𝑑𝑚𝑎𝑥 , is derived as the 95% lower confidence limit (LCL) of the HR for placebo versus the standard treatment. Non-inferiority of the new treatment versus the standard treatment is declared when the 2-sided 95% CI of the Bucher ITC comparing the new treatment vs the standard treatment is entirely below this margin. 

For example, when investigating non-inferiority of niraparib vs rucaparib in the ITT population, the reported HR and 95%CI for rucaparib vs placebo in ATHENA-MONO ( 𝐻𝑅𝑅𝑈𝐶𝐴 𝑣𝑠 𝑃𝐵𝑂 =0.47 [95% CI: 0.36 – 0.63]) are inverted to obtain a HR and 95% CI for placebo vs rucaparib ( 𝐻𝑅𝑃𝐵𝑂 𝑣𝑠 𝑅𝑈𝐶𝐴 = 2.128 [95% CI: 1.587 – 2.778]). In this example, 𝑑𝑚𝑎𝑥 =  1.587 and because the 95% CI for the effect of niraparib vs rucaparib from the Bucher ITC 𝐻𝑅𝑁𝐼𝑅𝐴 𝑣𝑠 𝑅𝑈𝐶𝐴𝐻𝑅𝑁𝐼𝑅𝐴 𝑣𝑠 𝑅𝑈𝐶𝐴 =XXX XXX XX XXX XXX is entirely below 𝑑𝑚𝑎𝑥 ￼, non-inferiority is established. 

Furthermore, we used Monte-Carlo simulation to estimate the probability that the HR for niraparib vs placebo, 𝐻𝑅𝑁𝐼𝑅𝐴 𝑣𝑠 𝑃𝐵𝑂 , is lower than the HR for the comparator vs placebo, 𝐻𝑅𝐶𝑂𝑀𝑃 𝑣𝑠 𝑃𝐵𝑂 . This simulation was conducted by drawing 1,000,000 values from two independent normal distributions, parameterized to match the reported hazard ratios (HRs) and their corresponding 95% confidence intervals. 

- A probability of 𝐻𝑅𝑁𝐼𝑅𝐴 𝑣𝑠 𝑃𝐵𝑂 < 𝐻𝑅𝐶𝑂𝑀𝑃 𝑣𝑠 𝑃𝐵𝑂 that is close to 50%, supports the hypothesis of non-inferiority as it reflects that the distributions of the reported HRs are indistinguishable. 

- A probability of 𝐻𝑅𝑁𝐼𝑅𝐴 𝑣𝑠 𝑃𝐵𝑂 < 𝐻𝑅𝐶𝑂𝑀𝑃 𝑣𝑠 𝑃𝐵𝑂 that is higher than 50% may indicate that the assumption of non-inferiority is conservative. 

- The probability of 𝐻𝑅𝑁𝐼𝑅𝐴 𝑣𝑠 𝑃𝐵𝑂 < 𝐻𝑅𝐶𝑂𝑀𝑃 𝑣𝑠 𝑃𝐵𝑂 will typically be lower than 50% when the reported HR in PRIMA/PRIME is higher than the reported HR in the comparator study. However, niraparib could still be non-inferior to the 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 616 -->

comparator treatment if both treatments are highly efficacious compared to placebo and the fixed margin analysis supports non-inferiority.

## _**Model structure**_ 

**B2. Priority question: As noted in Section A, in TA1055, analyses were presented in the HRp and HRd. As such, please update the model structure to include the following populations:** 

- **BRCAm (comparison with olaparib);**

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 623 -->

A comparison with olaparib for the BRCAm population was included in the submitted economic model and in the original submission dossier. 

As rucaparib is reimbursed for the HRd BRCAwt population alone and not for the entire HRd population, the BRCAwt subgroup is the most appropriate population for comparison with rucaparib, as it captures all relevant populations currently reimbursed for rucaparib (i.e., HRd BRCAwt and non-HRD-positive). As outlined in our response to clarification question A1, the additional restriction for non-HRD-positive patients (i.e., ineligible for bevacizumab maintenance) aligns with current clinical practice for PARPi monotherapies. 

Furthermore, results from the Bucher ITCs, clinical opinion, and the mechanism of action indicate comparable effectiveness between niraparib and rucaparib, regardless of biomarker status. 

**B3. Priority question: Based on the available trial data, the EAG considers PFS2 to be a key outcome that should be included in the economic model. The EAG notes that the model structure is already set up to include a PFS2 health state. Therefore, please incorporate data based on the EAG requested analyses from Section A to include PFS2 as a health state in the economic model. Through excluding this health state, the EAG does not consider the model structure to appropriately capture the key outcomes and impact of PARPis. Please also ensure that any updates to health state utility values and health care resource used in the PFS2 health state are described.** 

As stated in Section 3.3.2 of the CS, a 3-state model was utilised due to the lack of relevant PFS2 data in high-risk patients to conduct appropriate ITC analyses versus olaparib for the BRCAm population or rucaparib for the BRCAwt population. The inclusion of PFS2 was not expected to have a substantial impact on the model results as the treatment pathway following disease progression with PARPi monotherapy remains consistent irrespective of the first-line PARPi utilised. However, we have updated the economic model to include PFS2 data for niraparib from the PRIMA trial and have performed two additional scenario analyses utilising the 4-state model approach, with generalised gamma and 1-knot hazard spline models selected to extrapolate PFS2 for both populations (see 

Clarification questions

## _**Survival modelling**_ 

## **B11. Priority question. Based on the implementation of any of the EAG’s previously requested analyses in the economic model using hazard ratios derived from an ITC, please ensure that the application of the HR is only applied to extrapolated survival curves that support the proportional hazards assumption.** 

As described in our submission, all Bucher ITCs were exploratory, despite the significant limitations identified in the FA. Specifically, they were conducted as a means to provide an unadjusted and approximate relative effect of niraparib vs olaparib and rucaparib, despite the challenges in adjusting for baseline differences and the lack of availability of data on key effect modifiers. Apart from these limitations, we also acknowledge the limitation that the estimated relative effects estimated from Bucher ITCs may not be appropriate when the assumption of PH is violated. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 632 -->

For all the studies included in the ITC analyses, the assumption of proportional hazards was assessed using three methods: 

- **Log-cumulative hazard plots:** Under proportional hazards, the log(-log(S(t))) vs. log(time) curves for the treatment arms are parallel. Curves that cross or appear to converge or diverge over time may be indicative of violation of the PH assumption. The interpretation should weigh in the number of patients remaining, events or length of periods where the patterns are not parallel. For example, curves that cross very early but remain otherwise parallel may still support a PH assumption as the early crossing could be due to an insufficient number of events at that point. Similarly, crossing near the end of follow-up may be due to depletion of patients at risk and low event counts. 

- **Schoenfeld Residuals:** The PH assumption can also be assessed based on the Schoenfeld residuals derived from fitting a PH model. When the effect is constant over time, the residuals should be independent of time. This can be assessed based on the spline function (with 3 df) fitted to the residuals; a relatively flat pattern at 0 would provide support for proportional hazards. 

- **HR and Time Interaction:** The PH assumption can be assessed by checking for an interaction between the effect of treatment and time in a Cox regression model. A statistically significant interaction (with time or with log-time) indicates a change in the log-HR per unit of time which suggests that the PH assumption may not hold. 

The table below (Table 11) presents the conclusions from this investigation. The log cumulative hazard plots, Schoenfeld residual plots and the results from the Cox models with interaction between time and treatment are available in the Appendix (Proportional Hazards Assumption Testing).

## **B12. Priority question. In the company’s model, once patients have reached 10 years progression-free, it is assumed that 100% of patients are in long-term remission. Please clarify why it was assumed to apply to 100% of patients and explore the impact in a scenario analysis in which a lower proportion is implemented.** 

As highlighted in Sections 3.2 and 3.4.2 of the CS, the approach of assuming that all patients alive and progression-free at the cure time point are considered cured (i.e., follow general population mortality elevated by biomarker-specific excess mortality) is aligned with recent NICE appraisals (TA962 and TA946). Furthermore, as highlighted in Section 3.4.2 of the CS, the potential for long-term remission and functional cure is supported by both clinical experts from previous NICE appraisal (TA962, TA946), literature and UK clinical experts’ feedback received during the development of the CS. In addition, in the recent NICE appraisal for olaparib (TA962) and olaparib + bevacizumab (TA946), a cure time point of 5-7 years was deemed plausible, with UK clinical experts at the advisory board also highlighting that the probability of relapse after 7-10 years is highly uncommon (and fairly uncommon after 5 years). Nevertheless, a more conservative cure point of 10 years was adopted in the current CS, with a 100% cure proportion adopted given the use of the upper bound of cure points provided by clinical experts, and approach to cure assumptions considered in prior PARPi appraisals. 

An exploratory scenario analysis was conducted for both the BRCAm and BRCAwt populations, assuming that 95% (instead of 100%) of patients who are alive and progression-free at 10 years are deemed cured. The impact of these exploratory 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 635 -->

scenarios on niraparib INMB vs. olaparib (BRCAm) or rucaparib (BRCAwt) was minimal (see Table 20 for BRCAm and Table 21 for BRCAwt). 

## **B13. Priority question. In the economic model, once patients are considered to achieve long-term remission at 10 years, they receive general population mortality estimates. An excess hazard of 1.26 sourced from Mai 2009 was applied to the general population mortality in the BRCAm analysis only. Please clarify why an increased risk of death beyond the ‘cure’ point was assumed only to apply for the BRCAm group? Other than the precedent set in the previous NICE TAs, was this based on a systematic review of the evidence?** 

Although a formal systematic review was not performed, ad-hoc literature review was conducted to try and identify relevant sources to inform long-term excess mortality for patients without a BRCA mutation, with no appropriate evidence identified to use in the economic model for the BRCAwt population. A 1.26 HR was therefore applied only to the BRCAm population in line with prior appraisals for olaparib (TA962) and olaparib plus bevacizumab (TA946). However, an additional scenario analysis has been conducted applying the same excess mortality HR of 1.26 for the BRCAwt population, which had a limited impact on the results (see Table 21).

B16. Please provide scenarios in the model for each comparison whereby overall survival is not required to be capped by the chosen PFS curve and the choice of OS extrapolation curve is based on the best fitting model with PFS instead capped by OS rather than the other way. 

Thank you for the request; however, we don’t believe that application of capping from above with OS would be appropriate and may result in clinically implausible extrapolations for PFS. 

As indicated in Section 3.4.2 of the original CS and in line with prior PARPi appraisals, PFS was used to model the cure point given that PFS has more mature data vs. OS, thus expected to more accurately reflect the long-term plateau associated with a longterm remission assumption (i.e. a plateau not yet clearly present in the PRIMA OS data). 

All UK clinical experts interviewed indicated that cure was achievable in a PRIMA-like high-risk population, and that patients remaining progression-free after 7-10 years were highly unlikely to relapse, with a more conservative 10-year cure point adopted in the base case model (with 8 and 12-year cure points explored in scenario analysis). In addition, UK clinical experts also confirmed that only a small proportion of patients receiving PARPi maintenance in subsequent lines could achieve cure, which would not occur in clinical practice if patients previously received PARPi as 1L maintenance, implying that only patients remaining alive and progression free for a sufficient duration of time on 1L PARPi maintenance could be considered cured. 

If it is assumed that the mechanic of capping from above with OS should take precedence over the cure mechanic, this would likely result in higher than general population mortality being applied to patients alive and progression free after the cure point, contradicting the cure assumption supported by clinical experts and accepted in prior NICE appraisals. 

This is further validated by evidence from the PRIMA trial showing a negligible proportion of death events occur pre-progression; in the PRIMA trial in the overall population XXX of PFS events XXXXXX were for the reason of ‘death’ with the remainder due to disease progression. It is therefore inappropriate to model death 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 641 -->

events occurring exclusively from the pre-progression state as would be implied by the PFS curve being capped by the OS extrapolation. 

Furthermore, if it is assumed that the cure assumption mechanic should take precedence over capping from above with OS after the cure point (i.e. the OS capping from above mechanic only applies before the cure point), this would have no impact on the base case analysis (and either no impact or minimal impact on the scenario analyses) as the OS-PFS crossing points occur after the 10-year cure point. 

B17. Guidance in NICE DSU TSD 23 recommends using the ONS life tables from 2017-2019 due to the uncertainty about the long-term impact of COVID-19 on data beyond 2020. As such, please update the model to use the 2017-2019 ONS life tables **.** 

Although NICE DSU TSD23 guidance recommends use of 2017-2019 life table data, this was published in January 2024 likely prior to the availability of 2021-2023 life table data. Comparison of the differences in annual mortality probabilities (qx) by age for individuals 50 years and above (Figure 2) with 2017-2019 estimates shows that despite a consistent increase in mortality being observed in 2018-2020, 2019-2021 and 2020-2022 life tables across age groups (excluding age 73), this trend was not present in the latest 2021-2023 life tables where smaller overall differences were observed including lower mortality probabilities for several age groups, with comparable differences in mortality probabilities as seen for the 2016-2018 life tables. As such, the latest 2021-2023 life table estimates were used as a more recent source of life table estimates.

## **B18. Priority question. In regard to subsequent treatments (2L and 3L) listed in Tables 106 and 107 in Appendix C1.3, please clarify:** 

## **a. If these are all based on progression,** 

We can confirm that subsequent treatments listed in Tables 106 and 107 of Appendix C1.3 were based on progression. As per SAP Section 4.3.3.4 (if there are one or more progression dates) all the reported follow-up therapies were grouped into lines of therapies by comparing their reported start dates to the reported progression dates. 

Clarification questions

The follow-up therapies started prior to the first progression date following the start of - any follow-up therapy are grouped as the first line of follow-up therapy. The follow up therapies started after the first progression date and prior to the second progression date are grouped as the second line of follow-up therapy, and so on. As a result, patients may have more than one therapy within the same line. 

## **b. If patients in the placebo arm of PRIMA who received chemotherapy as 2L and then receive maintenance PARPi, is the PARPi classified as a 2L treatment or 3L treatment, i.e. are placebo patients receiving a PARPi listed as 2L receiving this as a maintenance therapy after chemotherapy at 2L or as a 2L treatment for their progressed disease?** 

It is dependent on whether disease progression happened between the 2L chemotherapy treatment and the initiation of PARPi as 2L maintenance therapy. If patients experienced disease progression after 2L chemotherapy but prior to initiating PARPi, then PARPi was classified as 3L treatment. However, if PARPi was administered after chemotherapy and no progression occurred between the two therapies, it was still classified as 2L maintenance treatment.

## _**Time to treatment discontinuation**_ 

B20. In the comparison against olaparib, the company informs TTD by PFS and AE discontinuations, as was used for rucaparib, where it is assumed that at 2 years only 10% of patients remain on treatment, resulting in a sharp drop in the TTD curve used in the model at this time point. The EAG notes that SACT data for olaparib shows that at two years, 33% of patients remained on treatment and 13% at 3 years. 

a. Please clarify why 10% was assumed appropriate in the base case 

As highlighted in Section 3.4.7 of the original CS, feedback from three UK clinical experts consulted by GSK at the advisory board for niraparib indicated an expectation that 5-10% of patients would continue after 36 months. Based on this feedback, an estimate of 10% was selected for the base case analysis for niraparib. Although clinical experts suggested that the proportion continuing treatment with olaparib and rucaparib may be higher due to the earlier stopping rule at 24 months and shorter overall treatment exposure, the 10% assumption was applied to both treatments as a conservative assumption, given that the potential concerns regarding cumulative toxicity and the associated risks of AML/MDS with prolonged use are present for all PARPi comparators. 

An alternative TTDD scenario was previously included as part of the submitted economic analyses (Table 66 of the CS) using the full extent of available olaparib SACT TTDD KM data before assuming 100% discontinuation, which reflects the observed 33% at two years and 13% at 3 years remaining on treatment in the olaparib SACT TTDD noted by the EAG (see Figure 78, Appendix J of the CS). 

## **b.** Please also provide a scenario in which the TTD curve from the SOLO-1 trial is used to inform TTD for olaparib 

An additional TTDD scenario analysis was also included in the original CS derived based on fitting a simple exponential model through the median time on treatment estimate available from SOLO-1. Although not directly using the SOLO-1 TTDD curve for olaparib, estimates produced by this approach were reasonable similar, albeit slightly lower, to those from the observed SOLO-1 TTDD data (e.g. 71.3% versus ~74% at 1 year, 3.6% vs ~5% at 3 years) with only a small proportion of patients remaining on treatment after 24 months similar to the observed SOLO-1 TTDD curve. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 645 -->

As such, this scenario is anticipated to produce reasonably similar (albeit slightly more conservative) results compared to using the SOLO-1 TTDD curve directly, and so an additional scenario analysis directly using the SOLO-1 TTDD curve has not been conducted.

B23. The company used the dose of niraparib based on SACT data combined with the RDI taken from the PRIMA trial. However, the RDI from PRIMA is likely to be correlated with the dosing used. Please clarify why it was considered appropriate to combine these data sources to estimate treatment costs? 

GSK agree with the EAG that RDI may be correlated with the starting dose. Therefore, within the submitted base-case, the RDI is indeed dependant on the starting dose received. 

As the individualised dosing approach for niraparib is now the standard clinical practice, as supported by clinical opinion as well as RWE, the SACT data for patients starting on the 200mg and 300mg doses were considered more appropriate than PRIMA data, where most patients (n=359) received the higher starting dose of 300 mg (due to the amendment in trial protocol; please see section 2.4.1 of the CS) , and only 125 (approximately one third) received a starting dose of 200 mg. 

The SACT data were then combined with the RDI for niraparib from PRIMA, as RDI data were not available from other RWE studies. To avoid or minimise potential bias associated with higher proportions of patients initiating niraparib treatment on the 300mg dose in the PRIMA trial, separate RDI inputs specific to the starting dose were derived from PRIMA, for patients starting on the 200mg and 300mg doses (see Table 47 of the CS) Consequently, higher RDI values were calculated and applied in the 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 647 -->

CEM for individuals starting on a 200mg dose compared to a 300mg dose (72.9% vs 62.3% for BRCAm, 74.3% vs 59.9% for BRCAwt). 

B24. The company stop applying any PFS health state costs beyond 7 years. However, the EAG notes that this was in line with the initial appraisal for niraparib, which assumed a ‘cure point’ at 7 years. As the point for long-term remission in the current model is based at 10 years, please clarify why this time point has not been used and provide a scenario analysis where this is applied? 

Thank you for highlighting the stopping rule for follow-up and monitoring costs for patients who remain progression free. We agree that the progression free related costs stopping time point should coincide with the ‘cure point’, thus we have updated the economic model base case to consider a stopping rule for follow-up and monitoring costs applied to patients who remain progression free for at least 10 years. However, please note that the application of a 10-year stopping rule had a very limited impact on the results (see Table 16 and Table 17).

An additional scenario analysis has been performed for both populations using the 2024 PSSRU estimate of £13,964 (subsequently inflated to 2024 prices) for general cancer patients (please see Table 20 and Table 21), which had a limited impact on the base case model analysis. 

B25. The niraparib SmPC states that blood pressure should be monitored weekly for the first two months, monthly for the remainder of the first year and periodically afterwards. Assuming that blood pressure measurements would be taken during the 1.33 consultant visits per month applied in the model for all progression-free patients on PARPi treatment, an additional scenario analysis was conducted for each population

including an additional 5.33 consultant outpatient visits as part of the initial one-off monitoring costs for niraparib to generate a total of 8 visits for the first two months of the model (please see Table 20 and Table 21). 

However, inclusion of additional consultant-led visit costs for all patients was expected to be conservative for niraparib given that in-person heart rate and blood pressure monitoring were not anticipated to necessarily require a consultant-led outpatient visit, and as noted in TA673 and in the niraparib SmPC, that home-based blood pressure monitoring is expected to be appropriate for a proportion of patients receiving niraparib. 

## _**Health related quality of life**_ 

B27. The EAG notes that minimal detail is provided in the CS on the regression analysis performed to obtain utility values used in the economic model: 

## a) Was the regression analysis pre-specified? 

Methods for all analyses were pre-planned and carefully reviewed prior to conducting the statistical analysis. 

## b) How was the model structure and final included variables decided upon? 

Base-case utility values shown in Table 45 of the original CS were determined using the best multivariable linear model selected from 24 potential models. Each model considered different combinations of: 

- the progression-free survival (PFS) status with either 2 states or 3 states as follows: 

   - 2 states: “progression-free” vs “progressed” 

   - 3 states: “progression-free” vs “first progression” (post PFS1and pre-PFS2) vs “second progression” (post-PFS2) 

- BRCA status: “BRCAm” vs “BRCAwt” vs “BRCAnd” 

- HRD status: “HRd” vs “HRp” vs “HRnd” 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 649 -->

- A composite variable for BRCA/HRD groups: 

   - “BRCAmut” (i.e. “BRCAm & HRDd/HRnd”) 

   - “BRCAwt/HRd” (i.e. “BRCAwt & HRd”) 

   - “BRCAnd/HRd” (i.e. “BRCAnd & HRd”) 

   - “HRp” (i.e. “BRCAwt & HRp”, or “BRCAnd & HRp”) 

   - “HRnd” (i.e. “BRCAwt & HRnd”, or “BRCAnd & HRnd”) 

- Treatment: Nira or Placebo. 

In these models, the post-baseline utility score was the dependent variable, while the baseline (BL) utility score, PFS state, treatment (trt), and BRCA/HRD groups were candidate independent variables. The models varied by the inclusion of the independent variables and interactions between the PFS state and treatment; i.e., for each of the two PFS statuses (2 or 3 states), a total of 24 models were constructed as follows:

To address the positive correlation of utility scores across repeated patient visits, the Generalized Estimating Equation (GEE) method was utilized, employing either a compound symmetry (CS) or autoregressive (AR1) correlation structure to ensure model convergence. The model chosen as the final one had the lowest quasiinformation criteria (QIC), a standard measure of model fit in the GEE approach. This final model included only PFS (i.e. with 2-states: progressed or not progressed) as a covariate for estimating base-case utility values. The resulting utility values from this model were uniformly applied to the health states, regardless of treatment arm.

## **Updated Cost-effective Model Results** 

## **Base-case results** 

The total and incremental costs, QALYs, and LYG, along with the incremental cost per QALY and incremental Net Monetary Benefit (NMB) for the base case with PAS discount, are presented below in Table 16 for BRCAm and Table 17 for BRCAwt population. In the BRCAm population, niraparib compared to olaparib resulted in cost savings of XXX,XXX with the PAS price for niraparib. The health outcomes were largely equivalent with only a very marginal difference in QALYs of XXXXXX due to nominal differences in AE incidence estimates applied. The resulting incremental NMB indicated niraparib to be highly cost-effective, amounting to XXXXXX at a willingnessto-pay threshold (WTP) of £30,000 per QALY when including the niraparib PAS price discount. 

For the BRCAwt population, niraparib compared with rucaparib resulted in cost savings of XXXXXX when including the niraparib PAS price discount, with marginally lower incremental QALYs of XXXXXX making niraparib dominant over rucaparib. The resulting incremental NMB was XXXXXX at a WTP of £30,000 per QALY, when including the niraparib PAS price discount.

## **Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

Results from the PSA for both the BRCAm (vs. olaparib) and BRCAwt (vs. rucaparib) population base-case analyses are presented in Table 18 and Table 19, using the PAS price for niraparib. The results demonstrate good consistency with the deterministic analysis and show that niraparib remains a cost-effective treatment strategy versus olaparib and rucaparib, resulting in cost savings. 

The cost-effectiveness plane for niraparib versus olaparib and versus rucaparib is presented in **Error! Reference source not found.** and 

, respectively. At a willingness to pay threshold of £30,000, niraparib has a 100% probability of being cost-effective compared with olaparib and rucaparib. The costeffectiveness acceptability curves of niraparib versus olaparib and versus rucaparib are not presented, since niraparib is cost-effective with 100% probability up to very large willingness to pay thresholds.

The results of the DSA for the 10 most influential parameters on incremental net monetary benefit are presented in **Error! Reference source not found.** for the BRCAm population (niraparib vs. olaparib) and in **Error! Reference source not found.** for the BRCAwt population (niraparib vs. rucaparib). The DSA outcomes indicate that the most influential parameters against olaparib included parameters determining PFS and TTDD for niraparib, the likelihood of AE discontinuations and treatment exposure for AE-related discontinuation for olaparib and niraparib RDI. Similarly, against rucaparib, the most influential parameters were the parameters determining the PFS parametric fit and TTDD for niraparib and the likelihood of AE discontinuations and treatment exposure for AE-related discontinuation for rucaparib.

## **Scenario analysis** 

Scenario analyses conducted showed that the base case analysis versus olaparib (BRCAm) and rucaparib (BRCAwt) is robust to variations in input parameters as outlined in Table 20 and Table 21. For the BRCAm population, greater than 10% variation from the base case INMB results was observed in scenarios where the PFS HR was changed (XXXX), label-based TTDD was assumed, olaparib median TTDD was used, assumed SACT OS HR, and assumed SACT OS TTDD. For the BRCAwt population, a variation greater than 10% from the base case INMB was only observed in two scenarios: when RDI for rucaparib was included and when Bucher ITC HRs from the ITT population were used. In all scenarios, niraparib remained less costly compared to olaparib (BRCAm) and rucaparib (BRCAwt), with all resulting INMBs being positive.

As described in Appendix J of the CS, the following UK clinical expert feedback was collected on expectations for niraparib long-term OS: 

- The first expert indicated OS expectations of around 28% for niraparib at 15 years 

- The second expert suggested survival would be somewhere between lognormal and generalised gamma at 10 years (~XXX-XXX) and 20 years (~XXXXXX), with a preference towards the log-normal model due to the PFS/OS crossing point at ~11 years, and suggesting OS may be closer to XXX at 10 years and XXX at 20 years. 

- Although estimates presented for each parametric model were capped by adjusted general population mortality, the third clinical expert struggled to recommend a parametric model suggesting that 30-year OS predictions may be too optimistic in general due to the underlying age of the patient population. 

- The fourth expert noted an expectation of 35-40% OS at 10 years, suggesting that OS of around 36% at 10 years and around 20% at 20 years would be reasonable, and stating a preference for spline models due to the PFS crossing point

<!-- page 740 -->

As all SACT OS parametric models converged with the chosen PFS base case model before 15 years (and therefore produced equivalent OS thereafter), predictions at 10 years were compared with clinical expect feedback on 10-year OS expectations for niraparib, which ranged between approximately XX-XXX. Only the exponential (XXXXX) and log-normal distributions (XXXXX) produced an estimate within this range OS at 10 years, with all remaining models providing estimates below the lower bound of clinical expert expectations. However, as the log-normal model provided a slightly better statistical fit and visual fit to the observed data, this model was utilised for scenario analysis exploring use of the SACT data for extrapolating niraparib OS.

|**Living with the condition**<br>**6. What is it like to live**<br>**with the condition? What**<br>**do carers experience**<br>**when caring for someone**<br>**with the condition?**|A diagnosis of ovarian cancer can be devastating, significantly affecting quality of life. The symptoms of the<br>disease itself, the process of diagnosis, then treatment and anxiety over the high chances of recurrence, all<br>impact patients and their families physically and mentally. The disease affects every aspect of their life – their<br>relationships, work, family life and social life.<br>Patients told us:<br>“Before I was actually given my diagnosis, a consultant told me “you’re going to need to start on your bucket list””<br>“I didn’t sleep for months after being told I had advanced ovarian cancer”<br>“When you have ovarian cancer you are not yourself - life revolves around the disease and in the very worst<br>moments you have no interest in your family, friends and general life outside of the disease and what it is putting<br>your body and mind through.”<br>“Quality of life is poor – reasonable at best when on treatment. There is a desire to cram as much into life as<br>possible due to not knowing what is going to happen next but being bound by the horrific side effects such as<br>complete exhaustion, severe pain, nausea and vomiting and mouth ulcers that make it almost impossible to<br>eat.”<br>“[my diagnosis] has had a huge impact on my family. From being someone who never had a day's sick leave in<br>25 years of working to being someone who needed help to get upstairs and at times was in a wheelchair- it was<br>a very difficult time for all of us.”<br>“Ovarian cancer has taken away everything that makes me a woman.”<br>“Catastrophic.  Up to the point of diagnosis, I was a fit and healthy person who lived a very active life.  It was<br>devastating when I was diagnosed particularly knowing the survival rate and the fact that there is no absolute<br>cure.  Initially, physically I needed care around the clock but once chemo started it seemed to clear symptoms<br>very quickly.  The mental impact has been the hardest as the dreaded outcomes are never far away from my<br>thoughts.  I made the decision to give up work as life has become very precious and the only way I can deal with<br>it, is to get normality back as much as possible. I am now back walking and playing tennis and leading an<br>active life as much as possible.”|
|---|---|

“The impacts on my life were life changing and dramatic as I was so ill and could do so little while waiting and waiting for a proper diagnosis and to start some kind of treatment.” “Ovarian cancer not only limits the time a woman has to live, it also limits what a woman is able to do with the time she has left.” Living with the anxiety of recurrence is difficult: “It is a constant worry and overhang in your life. One’s attitude to life changes. What are you planning for? What time frame? There is so much uncertainty. I was ‘no evidence of disease’ after my first round of chemo and then the cancer came back. There is no way of knowing how long gaps in treatment will be. It is hard to stay optimistic and live in the present.” “Even when I’ve been NED, I’ve worried a lot about recurrence. Every twinge is a worry. For a long time I couldn’t sleep, I was getting two hours a night and I had to beg for sleeping tablets as I couldn’t function. What if I’m living my life and the cancer’s growing?” “The fear of recurrence featured heavily in my thoughts, especially at night, and it affected my sleep. When I did recur, I didn’t trust my body anymore. It took me a lot longer to get over the shock than the original diagnosis. I wasn’t sure if I could still be strong and positive. Having got over the fear of dying from the disease, these thoughts returned with a vengeance. Living with OC now, with me being NED for over 6 years feels different as I take a maintenance drug which is very effective. It’s my parachute.” “I think the biggest concern is not knowing if or when another relapse will come.” “Even once the treatment is over it's not really the end, it's always there, it's always in the back of your mind.” “When you finish chemo, you feel like it’s taking the crutches away, it's ‘what now’?” Ovarian cancer impacts the family and loved ones of the woman diagnosed: “Life for both the patient and carer becomes totally consumed by the disease – when the next hospital appointment will be, managing side effects, organising childcare, sleepless nights – it is a vicious circle that never seems to end.”

|**Current treatment of the**<br>**condition in the NHS**<br>**7. What do patients or**<br>**carers think of current**<br>**treatments and care**<br>**available on the NHS?**|Patients told us about their experiences being treated for ovarian cancer using surgery and chemotherapy:<br>"The standard current treatment for ovarian cancer is debilitating, requiring extensive surgery and gruelling<br>repeated courses of chemotherapy. Many women like me are left with chronic bowel pain and disturbance (or a<br>stoma) after surgery and the chemotherapy leaves women with multiple long-term effects including peripheral<br>neuropathy, joint pains and fatigue, and many understandably suffer from a degree of post-traumatic stress<br>disorder.”<br>“There were points where I couldn't even get up and go to the bathroom. I'm a really independent person and<br>from somebody who's led a very full independent life, never having to depend on anyone for anything, all of a<br>sudden my daughters are bathing me and I’m having to be carried to the bathroom.”<br>“During chemo treatment the emotional anxiety of having OC is heightened by the physical issues experienced<br>with the chemo. Everyone’s symptoms with chemo will be different but I found each of my six month cycles of<br>chemo brutal, both physically and mentally.  The times between treatment are easier - but again the worry of<br>what the next blood test will show - has the CA125 increased? - is ever present. Waiting for scan results is<br>agony.”<br>“For me personally after the initial diagnosis and first lot of treatment I thought there is just no way I can do that<br>again. Chemotherapy is so tough.”<br>“I had such an awful time and my treatment journey wasn't very good. I suffered very badly from side effects.<br>And with all of that, I reached a really dark place. Physically it bashed me and it broke me, but it nearly broke me<br>mentally as well and emotionally, to the point where I wanted it all to end. I wanted life to end. It was my faith that<br>grounded me and got me through that really dark portion, but also the love that surrounded me.”<br>We can see that the impact of chemotherapy on patients and family is extreme, and being able to extend the<br>time between these treatments would benefit all.|
|---|---|

|**8. Is there an unmet need**<br>**for patients with this**<br>**condition?**|Niraparib being available at first line has improved the options available to women and should become part of<br>standard practice.<br>A choice of first line maintenance therapies should be available for all those diagnosed with ovarian cancer –<br>enhancing choice enables those diagnosed with ovarian cancer to have an improved progression free survival<br>which is important for a disease which reoccurs.<br>Although PARP inhibitors all utilise the same mechanism of action, they do so in different ways and as such<br>have different pharmacological profiles and side effects.<br>Clinicians should be able to choose and adapt the maintenance therapy based on the specific needs and toxicity<br>risks of each patient. Patients themselves need to have options for first-line maintenance therapies, with a range<br>of options available in case of significant side effects.<br>Giving a woman hope, through access to niraparib at first line, gives her whole family, and friends, hope too.<br>Earlier access would allow women more, and better, quality time with friends and family, with fewer side effects<br>than chemotherapy, with better mental health due to reduced anxiety.<br>Patients and their families told us:<br>“[We need] choice of treatment options rather than just being told which treatment you are being put on.  Patients<br>should be given more information to take away and read and assess before then consulting with your oncologist<br>and deciding which path to go.”<br>"I also am very concerned that treatment options in the UK depends on where in the UK a patient lives. That<br>cannot be right. We are a NATIONAL health service."<br>"I felt that the system was designed to assume that I have OC and I’ll be ill for a short period of time and then I’ll<br>die from it, so there’ s no point investing any time or energy into any recovery or quality of life.  It felt that I was<br>forgotten about as there just wasn’t anything in place to support me."<br>There is a need for options for women at first line: “The awful news there’s nothing else for you until it returns. I<br>begged for something to keep it at bay.”|
|---|---|

|**Advantages of the**<br>**technology**<br>**9. What do patients or**<br>**carers think are the**<br>**advantages of the**<br>**technology?**|Providing niraparib after first line chemotherapy allows families a period of stability which would be priceless to<br>both the patient, their family and carers giving them good quality time together and a chance to do important<br>things they wished to do before the patient became too unwell to do such things.<br>Patients who have taken niraparib tell us:<br>“I have been on both a PARP inhibitor - niraparib - and on Avastin. I felt positive knowing that there is data which<br>shows that these maintenance treatments can keep the cancer at bay. And indeed they did do so in my case for<br>some time.”<br>“AMAZING! Although I had issues with low platelets initially, once put on the right dose, I have no known side<br>effects.”<br>“As niraparib is a tablet, we are freed up from endless time at a chemotherapy unit and have more time to enjoy<br>life”<br>“For any woman with recurrent ovarian cancer and their family, this period off chemotherapy whilst still relatively<br>well, would be priceless.”<br>“Apart from the first three months on the PARP which was tough (side effects such as really bad nausea/fatigue<br>etc) I live a wonderful, manageable life. I still have to manage the fatigue, and stress of living with cancer, but can<br>plan short term things like holidays and trips with my family. I play tennis, I paint. I am able to celebrate important<br>life events of my children e.g. my son going to Uni. Plan adventures with them. Share another Christmas. Build<br>more memories with my children. Try and become a better person. Use my experiences of cancer and help<br>others.”<br>“After chemo maintenance treatments are so much easier and one of the massive positives is that as a result of<br>being on treatments is that your vitals are constantly being monitored and there is always someone to answer any<br>issues/ problems/symptoms. This ‘holds your hand’ as you move to your new world of normal.  Hugely<br>positive.  It’s hard when you come off these treatments as then the fear of it returning kicks in.”<br>“[Maintenance treatments are] much needed alternatives for bodies that need a break from chemo as it can keep<br>you stable especially if your situation is only controlled not cured."<br>“As I’ve had two recurrences, progression free survival is of utmost importance to me.”|

## **Key messages** 

- 

- **24. In up to 5 bullet** Ovarian cancer is a devastating disease for both patients and their families/ friends, with a poor prognosis **points, please summarise** for the many women diagnosed at a late stage. **the key messages of your submission.** • Patients and their families face a great deal of anxiety over treatment itself, and whether the disease will recur (which it does for most). Maintenance treatments offer patients more time between chemotherapy treatments. 

   - Ovarian Cancer Action supports new options being made available that can give women more good quality time with their families and friends. In order to improve survival rates we must ensure that more patients have access to the best available treatment, and at the earliest opportunity. These options are life-changing for the patients we see every day, offering hope for the future. 

   - Making sure there are options for maintenance treatment gives patients and their clinicians the opportunity to choose the most suitable treatment based on the individual and their current health. 

   - On the basis of patient feedback Ovarian Cancer Action believe that niraparib should continue to be available for this cohort, and should move to routine access.

## **Living with the condition** 

|**6. What is it like to live**<br>**with the condition? What**<br>**do carers experience**<br>**when caring for someone**<br>**with the condition?**|Ovarian cancer has a significant impact on quality of life. The majority of people are diagnosed at Stage III when<br>it has already spread outside of the pelvis. This means they can experience symptoms impacting their health and<br>quality of life, such as ascites.  Treatment is therefore aimed at minimising the burden of the disease and<br>maximising periods of wellness between treatments. As treatment lines are exhausted, those diagnosed fear<br>being told there is no more treatment available to manage their ovarian cancer.<br>The surgery undertaken is most usually a total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.<br>This operation can have long term effects on abdominal organs and particularly the bowel with associated<br>continence issues. This may mean having manage a stoma, either short or long term. It will result in immediate<br>surgical menopause. Associated issues include fatigue, possible chronic pain and changes to body image and<br>function affecting sexuality.<br>Long-term effects of chemotherapy treatment can include peripheral neuropathy which can limit both walking<br>mobility and ability to drive.<br>These physically and psychologically debilitating side effects can impact relationships, work and caring roles<br>permanently.<br>Living with ovarian cancer can be very isolating, due to its comparative rarity those diagnosed may not meet<br>anyone else with the same condition or facing the same issues of managing their cancer as a chronic condition<br>rather than aiming for a cure.<br>Those diagnosed live with the anxiety of possible recurrence. The time after treatment whereby patients are<br>under routine surveillance can be psychologically very hard to cope with. Our members report feeling adrift and<br>as if they are waiting for their disease to return.<br>Having a choice of maintenance treatment and continued input from oncology teams offers a significant<br>psychological benefit as well as physical health benefits. There is currently one first-line PARPi routinely<br>available for people with non-BRCA+/HRD ovarian cancer and this treatment would provide further options for<br>these patients in the first line setting for whom rucaparib is unsuitable.|
|---|---|

## **Living with the condition** 

|**6. What is it like to live**<br>**with the condition? What**<br>**do carers experience**<br>**when caring for someone**<br>**with the condition?**|Around 6,900 women are diagnosed with ovarian cancer in England each year and two thirds are diagnosed at a<br>late stage (stage III or IV) when the cancer is more difficult to treat. Survival rates for ovarian cancer trail those<br>for many other cancers.<br>Standard treatment involves surgery and chemotherapy, with chemotherapy either post-surgery or neoadjuvant.<br>In the majority of cases the disease returns after first line treatment. At this point treatment is no longer curative<br>and each further recurrence and subsequent round of platinum-based chemotherapy a woman goes through<br>increases her chance of becoming platinum resistant; at which point very few treatment options remain and<br>prognosis is extremely poor.|
|---|---|



Patient organisation submission 

[Niraparib for maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian, fallopian tube and peritoneal cancer after response to first-line platinum-based chemotherapy (review of TA673)] 3 of 11 



<!-- page 813 -->

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

The prospect of recurrence casts a shadow over the lives of many women. Fears around recurrence are compounded by the knowledge that there are limited treatment options for ovarian cancer, particularly for the around 50 per cent who do not have a BRCA mutation or are not HRD positive. Patients are aware of the high level of recurrence for ovarian cancer so would welcome options that may prevent a recurrence or offer more time between lines of chemotherapy which has the potential to prolong platinum - sensitivity. Target Ovarian Cancer’s Pathfinder research found that 60 per cent of those diagnosed with ovarian cancer report that it had a negative impact on their mental health. We also found high levels of unmet needs for support with patients reporting the need for support with feelings of isolation, issues relating to body image and sex and intimacy. _“It’s completely affected me. Body image, anxiety. My personality has change”’_ Woman with ovarian cancer. There are also practical implications of debilitating treatments rendering individuals unable to work or take part in regular day-to-day life.

Such<br>tumours are susceptible to treatment with PARP inhibitors (PARPi) that exploit<br>the presence of HRD in the tumour. The greatest degree of HRD is seen in<br>tumours with a BRCA mutation, approximately 20-25% of all high-grade<br>tumours, but also in a further 25% that have HRD without a BRCA mutation.<br>Since the publication of clinical trials with PARPi in 2018 and 2019, and their<br>subsequent licensing, there have been major improvements in progression-free<br>survival in these subgroups of patients using PARPi. These drugs are also being<br>used in tumours that do not exhibit HRD by current tests, but here the effect of<br>PARPi is less marked.<br>As a consequence of this, the ESMO guidelines (updated in 2023) and ESMO-<br>ESGO-ESP consensus statements (2024) have categorised high-grade tumours<br>into three groups; BRCA, HRD+/BRCA wild-type/ and non-HRD (also called<br>HRP). Maintenance therapy options are recommended within each of the groups<br>using either PARPi, alone, or combined with bevacizumab, or Bevacizumab<br>alone. Thus, most patients are now recommended one of these three<br>maintenance options.|

## **13. Do you expect the technology to provide clinically meaningful benefits compared with current care?** 

- Do you expect the technology to increase length of life more than current care? 

- Do you expect the technology to increase healthrelated quality of life more than current care? 

currently funded by the company that is very popular with patients and treating doctors. It has led to a substantial reduction in travelling by patients, the implementation in many centres of telemedicine clinics reducing the size of clinics and the dispatch of drugs by mail. 

The current use of PARPi has substantially increased progression-free survival. This was the primary endpoint for the trial.  In an updated analysis there was a more than doubling of the progression free survival at 5 years (22% versus 12% in the total population and 35% versus 16% in the HRD positive group). High levels of cross over to PARPi at relapse in the control arm made it difficult to show an overall survival benefit. 

If this technology became unavailable progression-free survival with first line treatment would revert to pre-PARPi times. The best old results from studies in 2011 with bevacizumab did not measure PFS at 60 months but overall survival can be estimated from the GOG218 trial (not ICON7 which reflects UK practice) and is less than 25% at 60 months. Thus, PFS would be less. It should be noted that although there were no OS differences in the PRIMA trial the OS at 5 years was around 44% in the overall population and 56% in the HRD subgroup. Whilst the population in PRIMA only includes responding patients at the time of randomisation, overall survival in the VELIA trial with veliparib that included all patients from the time of diagnosis was around 50%. Veliparib is a PARPi that has not been taken forward for licensing.  Thus, the inclusion of PARPi into clinical practice means that approximately twice as many patients will be alive at 5 years compared with previous trials that were performed in the pre-PARPi era. From the perspective of a patient an approximate 50% reduction in the risk of progression with twice as many patients progression-free at 5 years is clinical result that would be welcomed by all.

It should be noted that measurement of HRD is based on a Genomic<br>Instability score, determined largely through measurement of genomic scarring.<br>Generally patients with BRCA mutations have higher HRD scores that those with<br>BRCA- wild type tumours but there is overlap in both directions, so that some<br>patients with BRCA-wild-type tumours may have a higher score that another<br>patient with a BRCA mutation. About 50% patients have a score that has been<br>defined as a negative ‘cut-off’ (for the Myriad MyChoice assay- the test<br>performed in clinical trials, it represents the 95% CI around scores from<br>BRCAmutated tumours). It is unfortunately that this scoring has been<br>interpretated as a categorical variable positive and negative as there are patients<br>either side of the cut-off whose outcome on PARPi may differ from the predicted<br>HRD score.  In trials of both niraparib and rucaparib the PFS was improved in<br>the HRD negative (HRP) group and consequently rucaparib has already been<br>approved in this HRD negative or unknown group in situations where<br>bevacizumab is not appropriate (NICE TA1055). The results with niraparib are<br>very similar to those of rucaparib.|

## **Part 2: Key messages** 

In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

- •Maintenance treatment with niraparib significantly extends progression-free survival in a high-risk group of patients with advanced 

ovarian cancer. 

- •The beneficial effects are greatest in patients who have a tumour with a BRCA mutation but are also substantial in HRD positive BRCA- wild-type tumours. 

- •The benefit in HRD negative (HRP) tumours is modest and short-lived but can improve PFS particularly if bevacizumab is not appropriate. 

- The survival results at 5 years in the pivotal PRIMA trial are higher than has been seen in trials in the pre-PARPi era and the 

inclusion of niraparib maintenance represents a new and highly positive outcome result for patients with advanced ovarian cancer. 

- •The side effects of this oral drug are manageable with few patients needing to cease treatment due to adverse effects, 

Thank you for your time.
